title: Remembering the Future: Episodic Simulation, Mental Time Travel and the Affective Basis of Prospection

body:
Abstract

Episodic memory has traditionally been characterised as a system for retaining the past. Converging neuropsychological, neuroimaging and behavioural evidence has recast it as a system whose primary function may be prospective: supplying the materials from which possible future events are simulated. The present review examines this claim through Tulving’s account of autonoetic consciousness and chronesthesia, Suddendorf and Corballis’s mental time travel framework, and the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis of Schacter and Addis. We consider evidence from amnesic patients, from fMRI studies showing a shared core network for remembering and imagining, from overgeneral memory in depression, and from phenomenological and affective-forecasting work indicating that future simulations are emotionally weighted and that the ventromedial prefrontal cortex supports their affective content. We conclude that the loss of emotionally detailed episodic memory constrains not only recollection but the capacity to prospect, and derive requirements for any programme aiming to preserve human emotional memory: what must be preserved is not a record but the reconstructive, self-referential and affective components that permit recombination.

Keywords: episodic future thinking; mental time travel; autonoetic consciousness; constructive episodic simulation; default network; affective forecasting

1. Introduction

For most of the twentieth century, the study of memory was the study of retention; imagining the future was assigned to a separate faculty. This division was challenged from two sides. Clinically, Tulving (1985) reported that a densely amnesic patient was equally unable to recollect his past and to describe his following day. Theoretically, Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) proposed that mental travel into one’s own past and future is a single faculty whose adaptive value lies in the future. Schacter and Addis (2007) then supplied a mechanism: episodic memory is constructive precisely because its function is to permit flexible recombination of past elements into novel simulations.

The literature that followed, grouped under the label of episodic future thinking (Schacter, Benoit, & Szpunar, 2017), converges on three claims: that remembering and imagining depend on a largely shared neural core; that damage to that core impairs both; and that the simulations it generates are emotionally weighted in ways that guide decision. The present review organises the evidence around these claims and draws out a consequence often left implicit: if the affective quality of episodic memory gives simulated futures their motivational force, then the loss of emotionally detailed memory does not merely impoverish the past; it constrains the futures a person can represent. This changes what an effort to preserve emotional memory must preserve.

2. Theoretical Foundations

2.1 Autonoetic consciousness and chronesthesia

Tulving (1985) distinguished three forms of consciousness aligned with three memory systems: anoetic (procedural memory), noetic (semantic memory, knowledge of facts without any sense of when they were acquired) and autonoetic, which accompanies episodic memory and consists in the awareness of oneself re-experiencing an event in one’s personal past. He later introduced the term chronesthesia (Tulving, 2002) for the capacity to be aware of subjective time and to locate oneself within it, and framed it as bidirectional: what permits re-experiencing the past permits pre-experiencing the future.

2.2 Mental time travel

Suddendorf and Corballis (2007), extending their earlier formulation, proposed that mental time travel is a unitary ability built on a representation of the self, the ability to disengage from current perception, and a generative system for constructing scenarios. On their account, memory is episodic because a store of specific, contextually bound experiences is the raw material for constructing specific futures; their further claim that the ability is uniquely human remains contested.

2.3 The constructive episodic simulation hypothesis

Schacter and Addis (2007) turned an apparent flaw of memory into an explanation of its design. Recollections are assembled from fragments and are vulnerable to source confusions; on an archival view, these are pure costs. Schacter and Addis proposed instead that a system built to simulate future events must extract and recombine elements of past experience, and that this flexibility inevitably produces reconstruction errors. The hypothesis predicts overlapping neural systems for remembering and imagining, and impaired future thinking wherever episodic memory is impaired. On this view the brain is fundamentally prospective: stored information serves simulation rather than retention for its own sake. Addis (2020) has since reframed remembering itself as one instance of event simulation, differing from imagining chiefly in the constraints placed on the construction process.

3. Neuropsychological Evidence

3.1 Patient K.C.

K.C. sustained bilateral medial temporal lobe damage in a motorcycle accident in 1981. Intelligence, language and semantic knowledge of his own life were preserved, but he could not recollect a single personal episode. Tulving (1985) observed that when K.C. was asked what he would do tomorrow, he reported the same subjective blankness as when asked what he had done yesterday. The observation was informal, but it is the first documented dissociation between intact semantic knowledge and abolished autonoetic access in both temporal directions.

3.2 Patient D.B.

Klein, Loftus and Kihlstrom (2002) provided a systematic replication. D.B., a 78-year-old man rendered amnesic by anoxia following cardiac arrest, was severely impaired both on recollecting his own past and on imagining his own future. When asked about the future of public affairs, however, he answered coherently and comparably to controls. D.B. retained the concept of the future and could reason about it, but could not place himself within it. As with K.C., the evidence is a single case with non-standardised tasks, limiting generalisation but not the logic of the dissociation.

3.3 Hippocampal amnesia and scene construction

Hassabis, Kumaran, Vann and Maguire (2007) tested five patients with bilateral hippocampal damage using a paradigm that removed personal reference: participants imagined fictitious scenes cued by short prompts, for example lying on a white sandy beach in a tropical bay. Descriptions were scored for content and spatial coherence. Four of the five patients produced descriptions that were reduced in content and, most strikingly, fragmented: they named sand, sun and water but did not bind them into a scene one could occupy. The authors interpreted the hippocampus as providing the spatial scaffold within which details are integrated, whether the representation is a memory, a future event or a fiction. The deficit lies at the level of scene construction, on which both recollection and prospection depend. One patient performed normally, a reminder that lesion extent matters.

4. A Shared Core Network

4.1 Neuroimaging of remembering and imagining

Addis, Wong and Schacter (2007) provided the first direct fMRI comparison of past and future event generation, using matched cue words and separating construction from elaboration. Both conditions engaged a common set of regions: hippocampus and parahippocampal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex, and lateral temporal and parietal cortex. During construction, future events produced greater activity in right frontopolar cortex and anterior hippocampus, consistent with the added demand of recombining elements into a novel configuration. The overlap has been widely replicated; divergences concern the interpretation of the future-greater-than-past differences rather than the overlap itself (Schacter et al., 2017).

4.2 Self-projection and the default network

Buckner and Carroll (2007) noted that these regions coincide closely with those engaged by theory of mind and spatial navigation, and with the default network, active during rest and suppressed during externally directed tasks. They proposed that these tasks share a common process, self-projection: the shifting of perspective from the immediate environment to an alternative situation, whether past, future, another person’s or another place. On this view the default network is not idle but simulates situations that are not present.

5. The Affective Dimension of Prospection

5.1 Overgeneral memory and the impoverished future

Depressed and suicidal patients, given a cue word such as happy and asked for a specific memory, tend to respond with categorical summaries rather than single dated episodes. Williams et al. (1996) extended this overgeneral memory to the future. Parasuicidal patients who produced overgeneral memories also produced less specific and less imageable descriptions of future events, with the two measures correlated. In a second study, healthy participants trained to retrieve memories categorically then generated less specific future events than those trained to retrieve specifically. The induction result moves the relation towards causation and offers a cognitive account of the foreshortened future in depression. If specific, affectively textured memories are unavailable, the future cannot be populated with such scenes, and hopelessness becomes less a judgement than a representational vacancy.

5.2 Phenomenology of future thinking

D’Argembeau and Van der Linden (2004) asked healthy participants to generate past and future personal events varying in valence and temporal distance and to rate their sensory, contextual and emotional qualities. Future events contained fewer sensory and contextual details than past events, consistent with their being constructed rather than retrieved; positive events were richer in detail than negative events, and near events richer than distant ones. In later work the same authors found that individual differences in visual imagery and habitual emotion regulation predicted the phenomenological quality of both remembered and imagined events, with expressive suppression associated with less vivid representations in both directions. Emotion is thus a determinant of the vividness of future simulations, not an optional colouring.

5.3 Affective forecasting

Gilbert and Wilson (2007) reviewed evidence that people use prospection to preview the hedonic consequences of possible events, and that these affective forecasts are systematically biased because simulations are unrepresentative, essentialised and abbreviated. The relevant point here is the mechanism: the affective response to a simulated event is the signal by which the organism evaluates it, obtained by running the simulation and reading off the feeling it produces. Prospection is thus affective by design, and guides choice only if the simulation is detailed enough to elicit a discriminating emotional response.

5.4 The ventromedial prefrontal cortex

Benoit, Szpunar and Schacter (2014) examined the neural basis of this affective component. Participants imagined future events involving familiar places and people varying in how much they were liked. Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity tracked the imagined event’s affective value, and vmPFC connectivity with regions representing the constituent elements increased during integration. The authors interpreted vmPFC as integrating distributed knowledge about the elements of a simulation into a representation of its affective value.

6. Synthesis: Emotional Episodic Memory as a Constraint on Prospection

The evidence supports a chain of dependencies. Scene-like personal prospection depends on a construction process in the hippocampal-cortical core network; that process draws on stored episodic elements; and the resulting simulations acquire motivational force from an affective evaluation in which vmPFC is centrally involved. Hippocampal amnesia, overgeneral memory and habitual affective suppression show that degradation at different points in this chain produces a correspondingly degraded future. This is the thesis of the present review: the loss of emotional episodic memory constrains prospection in two ways, by removing the specific elements from which scenes are built and by removing the affective signal by which simulated scenes are evaluated. Such a person may retain the concept of the future, as D.B. did, but cannot populate it with self-involving, emotionally weighted episodes.

The claim requires caution. Most causal evidence comes from small patient samples or short-term inductions, the fMRI evidence is correlational, and the considerable role of semantic memory in future thought has not been reviewed here. Nor is the relation monotonic, since excessively vivid negative simulations are implicated in anxiety; the evidence establishes a dependency, not an optimum.

7. Implications for Emotion Preservation

A programme aiming to preserve human emotional memory must be assessed against a criterion that is not archival: not whether an experience has been recorded but whether what is retained can support the reconstructive, self-referential and affective operations by which episodic material becomes usable for prospection. Several requirements follow, stated as testable propositions.

First, preservation of semantic facts about emotional events is insufficient: K.C. retained the facts of his life and could not use them to imagine a future. A preserved representation should be evaluated on whether it supports scene construction, measurable by the scoring of Hassabis et al. (2007), rather than on factual completeness.

Second, specificity is a preservation target in its own right, since categorical summaries do not support future imagery and specific episodes do. Interventions restoring access to specific episodes should therefore improve the specificity of future thinking; strategies which abstract or summarise experience should not.

Third, affective detail must be preserved together with perceptual and contextual detail, since emotional intensity and sensory richness covary and affective value is computed by integrating the elements of a scene. A representation stripped of its emotional component should yield simulations that are constructed but not evaluated, and hence inert for decision.

Fourth, the autonoetic component, the sense of oneself within the scene, is the least understood and most fragile; D.B.’s dissociation shows it can be lost while temporal reasoning survives. Whether any external trace can re-instate rather than merely cue it is an open question that a preservation programme should treat as central.

Finally, the goal is not fidelity. A perfectly reproduced episode has limited prospective value; what matters is whether its elements remain available for recombination. Preservation should be judged by the futures it makes constructible.

8. Conclusion

The reorientation of memory research towards prospection has replaced the picture of episodic memory as an archive with one of a generative resource. On this picture, the observation that amnesic patients cannot imagine tomorrow, and that depressed patients imagine it only in outline, is a direct expression of the system’s design. The affective findings sharpen the point: emotion is how a simulated event is evaluated, and its vividness depends on the vividness of the memory from which the simulation was built. For a foundation concerned with preserving emotion, the consequence is that emotional memory is worth preserving not only for what it holds of the past but for what it makes possible in the future; the two cannot be separated without losing both.

title: Emotional Memory Across the Lifespan: Positivity Effects, Reminiscence and Preservation in Dementia
description: Does emotional memory decline with age as episodic memory does, or does it follow a distinct trajectory? The present review examines three bodies of evidence. First, socioemotional selectivity theory and the age-related positivity effect indicate that older adults…
body:
Abstract

Does emotional memory decline with age as episodic memory does, or does it follow a distinct trajectory? The present review examines three bodies of evidence. First, socioemotional selectivity theory and the age-related positivity effect indicate that older adults preferentially attend to and remember positive material, a shift that a meta-analysis of 100 studies attributes to motivated, resource-dependent processing rather than neural decline. Second, research on reminiscence and life review shows that recollection in later life is functionally heterogeneous and that its benefits depend on which function is engaged; the reminiscence bump identifies early adulthood as the period from which emotionally salient memories are most densely retrieved. Third, studies of amnesia and Alzheimer’s disease demonstrate that the experience of an emotion can outlast declarative memory for the event that induced it. We conclude that emotional memory in ageing is selected, reconstructed and partly dissociable from event memory. For emotion preservation, this implies that what should be captured is not a neutral record of events but the affective trace the person has built around them, and that this trace remains ethically consequential when the record itself is no longer accessible.

Keywords: positivity effect; socioemotional selectivity; reminiscence; life review; reminiscence bump; Alzheimer’s disease

1. Introduction

The dominant framework for cognitive ageing describes monotonic decline in fluid abilities, episodic memory and processing speed. Emotional functioning does not fit this picture: surveys consistently report that negative affect decreases from early adulthood to at least the seventh decade while positive affect and life satisfaction remain stable, the so-called “paradox of well-being” in old age. Memory researchers have documented age-related changes in what is remembered, and clinical neuropsychology has shown that emotional experience may persist when the declarative record of its cause is gone.

These literatures have developed largely in isolation. The present review brings them together around one question: what is the status of emotional memory in the ageing individual, and which of its properties would a preservation effort need to respect? Section 2 reviews the positivity effect and its replication status; Section 3 examines reminiscence as function and intervention, and the temporal distribution of autobiographical memory; Section 4 considers the dissociation of emotion and memory in amnesia and Alzheimer’s disease; Section 5 translates the findings into requirements for preservation.

2. Motivated cognition in later life

2.1 Socioemotional selectivity theory

Carstensen, Isaacowitz and Charles (1999) proposed that the perception of time remaining in life, rather than chronological age as such, organises the goals people pursue. When time is perceived as open-ended, knowledge-related goals dominate: acquiring information, expanding social networks, preparing for a distant future. When time is perceived as limited, emotionally meaningful goals take precedence: present affective states, close relationships and the regulation of emotion. Because age is strongly correlated with perceived time horizon, older adults typically show the second profile.

The theory predicts that manipulating time horizon should shift goals independently of age. Younger adults facing life-limiting illness or political instability show the preference for familiar over novel social partners that characterises older adults; asking older adults to imagine an extended future reduces that preference (Carstensen et al., 1999). Age-related emotional change is thus adaptive reprioritisation rather than a by-product of loss.

2.2 The positivity effect

Mather and Carstensen (2005) extended the theory to cognition, arguing that the same motivational shift should bias attention and memory towards positive information. In the anchoring memory study, Charles, Mather and Carstensen (2003) presented young, middle-aged and older adults with positive, negative and neutral pictures under incidental encoding and later tested free recall and recognition. Recall of negative images decreased across age groups, whereas memory for positive images was relatively spared, so the ratio of positive to negative images remembered increased with age. Eye-tracking and dot-probe studies showed a parallel attentional bias.

Two features are theoretically decisive. The effect depends on cognitive control: under divided attention, or when older adults are instructed to attend to negative content, it is reduced or abolished. And older adults with better executive function show it more strongly, not less, which is difficult to reconcile with amygdala or frontal decline. The effect therefore appears to reflect goal-directed regulation rather than an inability to process negative material (Mather & Carstensen, 2005; Carstensen & DeLiema, 2018).

2.3 Replication and boundary conditions

The positivity effect has seen failed replications and disputes over its magnitude. Reed, Chan and Mikels (2014) meta-analysed 100 studies comparing younger and older adults on preferences for positive over negative information and reported a reliable overall age difference in the predicted direction, of small magnitude. Crucially, the effect was substantially larger in studies that left participants free to process stimuli as they wished than in studies imposing instructions, time limits or divided attention, in which it approached zero. This is what a motivational account predicts and a deficit account does not.

Two limitations remain. Most evidence is cross-sectional, so cohort effects cannot be excluded, and the effect concerns relative preference: with threat-related or highly arousing stimuli the bias often disappears. The established finding is that, when unconstrained, older adults allocate memory resources preferentially to positive material; the shift is modest and depends on available control resources.

3. Reminiscence, life review and the structure of autobiographical memory

3.1 From clinical observation to functional taxonomy

Butler (1963) reframed the tendency of older people to revisit their past, then widely regarded as a symptom of decline, as a normative and potentially adaptive process: the approach of death prompts a return to consciousness of past experiences, particularly unresolved conflicts, which are re-examined and, under favourable conditions, reintegrated. The outcome is not uniformly positive; life review may result in acceptance, but also in guilt, anxiety or depression when reintegration fails. The formulation was clinical and unquantified, but it set the agenda for five decades.

Webster (1993) supplied the psychometric structure. The Reminiscence Functions Scale, validated on a sample spanning late adolescence to old age, identified eight factorially distinct reasons for recalling the past: boredom reduction, death preparation, identity, problem solving, conversation, intimacy maintenance, bitterness revival and teaching or informing others. Subsequent work has repeatedly found that bitterness revival and boredom reduction predict poorer mental health, whereas identity, problem solving and the prosocial functions predict better adjustment.

Westerhof and Bohlmeijer (2014), reviewing fifty years of research, distinguished simple reminiscence (unstructured, conversational), life review (structured, evaluative, integrative) and life-review therapy (life review directed at psychopathology), and noted a shift from asking whether reminiscence is beneficial to asking which functions, for whom, and under what conditions.

3.2 Interventions: meta-analytic evidence

Pinquart and Forstmeier (2012) meta-analysed 128 controlled studies of reminiscence interventions. Moderate improvements were found for depressive symptoms and ego integrity (Hedges’ g in the region of 0.6), with smaller but significant effects on purpose in life, death preparation, mastery, well-being and social integration. Effects on depression were larger for life-review therapy than for simple reminiscence and in participants with clinically relevant depression at baseline, and were maintained but attenuated at follow-up. Study quality was variable and moderator analyses rest on few studies. Nonetheless, structured recollection of the emotional past produces measurable changes in affective state, and structure and integration, rather than recollection per se, carry the effect.

3.3 The reminiscence bump

When adults over about forty produce autobiographical memories, their distribution across the lifespan shows a marked over-representation of memories from roughly ages 10 to 30. Rubin, Rahhal and Poon (1998) showed that this reminiscence bump is not restricted to personal episodes: older adults also disproportionately date their favourite films, books and music to this period, name public events from it as most important, and perform best on knowledge of news and cultural items from it. Early adulthood thus appears to be a privileged period of encoding whose products are retained across life.

Explanations are not mutually exclusive: novelty produces distinctive encoding; identity formation makes these memories central to the self and frequently rehearsed; and culturally shared life scripts guide retrieval towards the period when important, largely positive, transitions are expected. Across explanations, the bump is dense in emotionally significant, self-relevant and predominantly positive events, and thus indicates where in a life the affectively central material is most likely to be found.

4. Emotion without memory: amnesia and Alzheimer’s disease

4.1 Sustained feeling after loss of the inducing event

Feinstein, Duff and Tranel (2010) tested whether an emotional state requires memory of its cause in order to persist. Five patients with severe amnesia following bilateral hippocampal damage, and matched healthy participants, watched film clips inducing sadness and, in a separate session, happiness, with emotional state rated at intervals over the following half hour. The patients retained little or no memory of the clips, several failing to recall that they had watched a film at all. Nonetheless their sadness persisted for twenty to thirty minutes, comparable to or exceeding that of controls, and its persistence was inversely related to the amount remembered; happiness also persisted, though less consistently. The experience of an emotion thus does not depend on the declarative record of the event.

Guzmán-Vélez, Feinstein and Tranel (2014) replicated the design in patients with probable Alzheimer’s disease and healthy older adults. The patients forgot the film content within minutes, yet both sadness and happiness remained elevated throughout the observation period, and poorer memory was again associated with more prolonged sadness. The authors framed the result as “feelings without memory” and drew the clinical implication directly: interactions a patient will not remember can nevertheless produce durable emotional consequences in either direction. The finding is consistent with a neuropathology in which medial temporal structures supporting episodic memory are affected early while circuits supporting affective response are comparatively preserved. Both studies rest on small samples and laboratory induction, and neither identifies the mechanism maintaining an unattributed emotion; the direction of the effect, however, has been replicated across two aetiologies.

4.2 Emotional enhancement of memory in Alzheimer’s disease

A distinct question is whether emotional content still enhances memory when memory itself is impaired, as it does in healthy adults through amygdala modulation of hippocampal consolidation. Kensinger, Anderson, Growdon and Corkin (2004) examined memory for emotional words in Alzheimer’s disease relative to healthy older adults. The enhancement observed in controls was attenuated in patients, and in some conditions absent, depending on stimulus type and retrieval measure. Emotional enhancement appears to require an interaction between amygdala and medial temporal systems: when the hippocampal component is compromised, the amygdala continues to generate affective responses at encoding but can no longer confer an advantage on consolidation. This reconciles the two sets of findings: in Alzheimer’s disease, emotion is experienced and sustained, but it no longer reliably rescues the memory of what caused it.

4.3 Autobiographical memory and its emotional residue

El Haj, Antoine, Nandrino and Kapogiannis (2015) reviewed autobiographical memory in Alzheimer’s disease and characterised a shift from episodic to semantic retrieval: patients increasingly produce general or schematic memories in place of specific, contextually detailed episodes, with a temporal gradient sparing remote over recent periods; memories from the reminiscence bump are among the most resilient. The same group has reported that self-selected music increases the specificity and emotional content of autobiographical retrieval in mild Alzheimer’s disease, such memories being predominantly involuntary and positive. What survives longest in the autobiographical record of a person with dementia thus appears to be a small set of remote, emotionally weighted, self-defining memories, most readily reached through affectively charged cues rather than direct questioning. Most of these studies are small and await replication.

5. Implications for emotion preservation

The evidence reviewed can be stated as constraints on any preservation programme.

First, the emotional record of an older adult is a selected record. The positivity effect and the functional analysis of reminiscence show that what is retained and rehearsed reflects current goals, particularly affect regulation. Treating this selection as distortion to be corrected would misdescribe the object. We propose as a requirement that preservation capture the person’s evaluative stance towards an event alongside the event itself, and record the circumstances of retrieval (spontaneous or cued, conversational or evaluative) as part of the data.

Second, emotional memory is partly dissociable from event memory, and the affective component is the more durable. This yields a testable proposition: material collected from an individual before cognitive decline, if it encodes emotional appraisal and not only factual content, should continue to elicit corresponding affective responses after episodic access to the underlying events is lost. The reminiscence bump specifies where such material is most likely to be found, and the music findings in Alzheimer’s disease suggest which cue modalities are most likely to reach it.

Third, eliciting emotional memory is not neutral. Structured, integrative recollection improves affective outcomes, whereas recollection oriented towards bitterness predicts poorer adjustment. Elicitation protocols used for preservation should therefore be designed and evaluated as interventions, with the function engaged as an independent variable and well-being as an outcome.

Fourth, the persistence of unattributed emotion in dementia imposes an ethical constraint that precedes any collection. A person who cannot remember an interaction still bears its emotional consequences. Preservation activities involving people with dementia must be assessed for their affective footprint on the participant, not only for what is obtained. Open questions include whether preserved affective material can be transmitted to another person in a form that reproduces rather than describes the emotion, and how consent for such transmission should be understood when the source can no longer evaluate it.

6. Conclusion

The three literatures reviewed here describe one system from different angles. Socioemotional selectivity accounts for why older adults reorganise memory around emotional value; the reminiscence literature describes how that reorganisation is enacted in recollection and to what effect; and the dementia studies show what remains when episodic memory fails. The picture is of an emotional memory that is motivated, functionally differentiated and more robust than the events it accompanies. Several central findings rest on small or cross-sectional samples. Integrating experimental, gerontological and neuropsychological methods within longitudinal designs is the most direct route to establishing which properties of emotional memory are invariant across the lifespan and which depend on the goals, resources and health of the remembering person.

title: External Memory Systems: Cognitive Offloading, Transactive Memory and What Records Fail to Encode

body:
Abstract

Humans have delegated memory to external supports since the invention of writing, and the concern that such delegation weakens internal memory is at least as old as Plato’s Phaedrus. The present review asks what contemporary evidence says about the cognitive consequences of externalising memory and about the limits of what records can preserve. We examine the extended-mind hypothesis and its critics, Wegner’s transactive memory framework, the “Google effect” and its replication status, cognitive offloading, the photo-taking-impairment effect and its boundary conditions, saving-enhanced memory, and lifelogging research with wearable cameras in amnesic patients. The evidence indicates that external storage reliably shifts encoding strategy, sometimes at a cost to content memory and sometimes to its benefit, with effects moderated by intention, control over what is captured, and the reliability of the store. Critically, no recording medium encodes the affective, interoceptive and self-referential components of experience; records act as retrieval cues for such states rather than as copies of them. For a programme of emotion preservation, this implies that the target cannot be the record alone but the coupling between record, rememberer and social partners.

Keywords: cognitive offloading; transactive memory; extended mind; autobiographical memory; photo-taking impairment; lifelogging

1. Introduction

The question of whether external memory aids strengthen or weaken the mind predates experimental psychology by more than two millennia. In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates relates the myth of Theuth, who presents writing to King Thamus as a remedy (pharmakon) for memory. Thamus replies that writing will produce forgetfulness, because those who trust external marks will cease to exercise their own memory; what has been invented is an aid to reminding, not to remembering (Plato, trans. 1995). The passage is notable for the distinction it draws between internal memory and externally cued recollection, and for its claim that the effect operates through trust in the external store. Both ideas recur in the empirical work reviewed below.

The contemporary literature is fragmented across philosophy of mind (Clark & Chalmers, 1998; Adams & Aizawa, 2001; Rupert, 2004), social psychology (Wegner, 1987; Sparrow, Liu, & Wegner, 2011), cognitive psychology (Henkel, 2014; Storm & Stone, 2015; Risko & Gilbert, 2016; Barasch, Diehl, Silverman, & Zauberman, 2017) and human–computer interaction (Hodges et al., 2006; Sellen & Whittaker, 2010; Loveday & Conway, 2011). The present review integrates these strands around two questions: what does externalising memory do to the internal memory of the person who externalises, and what dimensions of experience do external records systematically fail to encode? We argue that the first question has a defensible but heavily moderated answer, whereas the second has been underexamined and bears directly on any attempt to preserve emotional memory.

2. Where does memory end? The extended mind and its critics

Clark and Chalmers (1998) proposed that cognitive processes are not confined to the skull. Their central illustration contrasts Inga, who recalls a museum’s address from biological memory, with Otto, a patient with Alzheimer’s disease who retrieves the same address from a notebook he always carries. Because the notebook is reliably available, automatically consulted, readily endorsed, and was endorsed at the time of entry, the authors argued that it plays the same functional role for Otto as biological memory plays for Inga and should count as part of his memory. The claim is a parity argument: a process that would count as cognitive in the head should not be excluded merely because it occurs outside it.

The hypothesis has been contested on two main grounds. Adams and Aizawa (2001) argued that cognition is marked by non-derived content and a distinctive causal profile, which notebooks lack; coupling a cognitive system to an external resource does not make the resource cognitive, a move they call the coupling-constitution fallacy. Rupert (2004) objected on empirical grounds: internal memory exhibits regularities such as primacy, recency, interference and generation effects that external stores do not, so a science that treated Otto’s notebook as memory would lose explanatory generalisations. He proposed a weaker “embedded” view, on which cognition depends heavily on external resources without being constituted by them.

The outcome of this debate matters less here than the conditions it makes explicit. Clark and Chalmers’ criteria of availability, automatic reliance, endorsement and prior authorship specify when an external store becomes functionally integrated. Rupert’s objection specifies what is lost when it does: the store lacks the consolidation, reconstruction and affective modulation that characterise biological memory. Both points bear on cases where the externalised material is not an address but an emotionally significant episode.

3. Distributed memory: from transactive systems to search engines

3.1 Transactive memory

Wegner (1987) proposed that close partners and small groups develop transactive memory systems: differentiated stores in which each member holds some information and, crucially, metamemory about what the others know. The system can retain more than its members individually, provided directory information (“who knows what”) is accurate and retrieval from partners is reliable. Wegner also noted its vulnerability: losing a partner through separation or bereavement is a loss of memory access as well as of relationship. The framework is descriptive rather than mechanistic, but it introduced the idea that encoding is sensitive to expectations about external availability.

3.2 The Google effect and its replication

Sparrow et al. (2011) extended this framework to information technology in four experiments. Participants who typed trivia statements into a computer and were told the entries would be saved recalled fewer statements than those told they would be erased; participants primed with difficult questions showed slower colour-naming of computer-related words in a modified Stroop task, interpreted as activated thoughts of search; and when statements were saved into named folders, participants remembered folder locations better than the statements. The authors concluded that the internet functions as a transactive partner and that people preferentially encode where information can be found rather than the information itself.

The replication record is mixed. The Social Sciences Replication Project (Camerer et al., 2018), which ran high-powered replications of 21 experiments published in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015, included one experiment from Sparrow et al. (2011) and did not obtain a significant effect in the original direction. Because only one of the four experiments was tested, the outcome does not invalidate the paper, but the claim selected for replication should be treated as unestablished. The broader pattern, that expected external availability reduces encoding effort, has convergent support from paradigms reviewed below.

4. Cognitive offloading as strategy

Risko and Gilbert (2016) proposed that the use of external action to reduce internal processing demand, which they term cognitive offloading, should be studied as a metacognitively controlled behaviour rather than an incidental consequence of technology. The decision to offload depends on the perceived cost of internal processing, the perceived reliability of the external resource, and confidence in one’s own memory. Paradigms include intention-offloading tasks in which participants may set reminders for delayed actions, and tasks in which a display can be rotated physically rather than mentally. People offload more when they judge their internal capacity to be low, and somewhat more than optimal performance requires, suggesting a bias toward externalisation when it is cheap.

Two consequences follow. First, offloading is not intrinsically detrimental: delegating a reminder frees capacity and improves prospective-memory performance. Second, the effect on subsequent internal memory depends on what offloading does to encoding. Storm and Stone (2015) found that saving a file of to-be-remembered items before studying a second file improved memory for the second file, a “saving-enhanced memory” effect that disappeared when saving was unreliable. Offloading, on this account, releases resources for subsequent encoding, but only when the store is trusted. The dependency on reliability echoes both Clark and Chalmers’ endorsement criterion and Plato’s diagnosis that the effect of writing operates through trust.

5. Recording experience: cameras, photographs and lifelogs

5.1 The photo-taking-impairment effect

Henkel (2014) had participants tour a museum, either observing designated objects or photographing them. The following day, photographed objects were recognised less accurately, and fewer visual details and locations were recalled, than objects that had only been observed. In a second experiment, photographing a specific detail by zooming in eliminated the impairment and preserved memory for the whole object, indicating that attentional engagement during capture, not the camera itself, drives the effect. Samples were modest.

Barasch et al. (2017) reported an important boundary condition. When participants chose freely what to photograph, memory for visual aspects of the experience was enhanced relative to no-photo controls, while memory for concurrent auditory information was impaired. Volitional photography thus appears to direct visual attention toward the scene at the expense of other modalities rather than uniformly reducing encoding. The effect of recording therefore depends on the agency and attentional stance of the recorder and on which sensory channel the record captures.

5.2 Lifelogging and SenseCam

Continuous capture pushes externalisation to its limit. Hodges et al. (2006) introduced SenseCam, a wearable camera that automatically photographs the wearer’s field of view at short intervals or when sensors detect changes in light, motion or heat. An initial case study with a severely amnesic patient showed that periodic review of SenseCam images supported retention of autobiographical events over months, whereas a written diary did not. Loveday and Conway (2011) examined a further amnesic patient and reported that image review gave access to otherwise inaccessible everyday memories, and that the images acted as cues triggering recollective experience, including sensory and emotional details not visible in the images themselves, rather than merely supplying facts about the day. They interpreted this within Conway’s model of autobiographical memory, in which event-specific knowledge remains stored but requires appropriate cues for access.

Sellen and Whittaker (2010) offered a constructive critique of the lifelogging programme. They argued that “total capture” conflates recording with remembering, that autobiographical memory serves functions (recollecting, reminiscing, retrieving, reflecting, remembering intentions) that an archive does not automatically serve, and that a lifelog is at best a set of cues whose value depends on the rememberer’s capacity to reconstruct from them. Indiscriminate capture also creates a retrieval problem: the more stored, the harder it is to find what matters.

6. What records fail to encode

Across these paradigms, the record is treated as a stand-in for the memory. The lifelogging literature shows this to be a category error. Autobiographical remembering is a reconstructive process that reinstates aspects of the original encoding state, including bodily and affective components. An image records the light that reached a lens; it does not record interoceptive state, the felt significance of the scene, the goals active at the time, or the self-relevant appraisal that determines whether an event is later judged central to identity. Loveday and Conway’s (2011) observation that SenseCam images elicited emotional and sensory details absent from the images is instructive: the affective content was retrieved from the rememberer, not from the record.

Three further limitations follow. First, recording alters the experience recorded: capture redistributes attention across modalities and can disengage the recorder from the scene. Second, records are selective in ways the recorder may not control. Clark and Chalmers’ endorsement criterion presupposes that the person authored the store; automatically curated archives violate that condition, so the resulting system is embedded rather than extended in Rupert’s (2004) sense. Third, transactive systems depend on partners who shared the experience and can be interrogated. A human partner remembers what was felt and can renegotiate the account; a store returns what was entered.

7. Implications for emotion preservation

The literature reviewed constrains any programme that aims to preserve emotional memory, and the constraints can be stated as testable propositions.

First, a record of an emotional episode is not the emotional memory; it is a cue. The preservation target should therefore be the reliability with which a record reinstates the affective state and self-relevant appraisal of the original episode in a rememberer, not the fidelity of the record to the scene. This predicts that records enriched with the rememberer’s own contemporaneous appraisal will cue emotion more reliably than higher-resolution records without it.

Second, capture must not degrade encoding of the components it cannot capture. The photo-taking findings predict that procedures requiring attentional selection by the person, as in Henkel’s zoom condition and Barasch et al.’s volitional condition, will produce less impairment than passive or directed capture, and that capture of one modality will impair memory for others unless the procedure deliberately samples them.

Third, authorship and endorsement matter. Following Clark and Chalmers and the saving-enhanced memory results, stores that the person fills and trusts should support subsequent encoding, whereas stores perceived as unreliable or externally curated should not. This is testable by manipulating perceived reliability and authorship of the archive.

Fourth, emotional memory has historically been distributed across social partners. A preservation programme should evaluate whether records function as shared cues within a transactive system and support reconstruction of an episode between people, rather than substituting for the partner; records may be most valuable when they preserve the directory information a lost partner held.

Finally, the replication history of the Google effect counsels modesty: claims about external stores and internal memory should be tested with preregistered, adequately powered designs before informing practice.

8. Conclusion

Thamus’s objection to writing, that trust in an external mark reduces the exercise of memory, has a partial empirical descendant: expected external availability changes what is encoded, and directed recording can thin memory for the recorded scene. But the evidence does not support a general degradation account. Offloading releases capacity, reliable saving improves subsequent learning, volitional photography enhances visual memory, and reviewed images restore access to episodes in amnesia. What unites the findings is that the effect of an external store depends on the coupling between store and rememberer: reliability, authorship, attentional stance at capture and the availability of partners who shared the episode. The dimension no record captures, the felt state of the person who was there, is also the dimension that gives an episode its value. An account of external memory that omits it describes archives, not remembering.

title: Why Preserve Emotions? A Cognitive Science Case for Treating Affective Experience as Perishable Data

body:
Abstract

Human societies have never produced more durable records of their members’ lives, yet almost none document what those lives felt like from the inside. This position paper asks whether affective experience is a category of information systematically lost by conventional archives and, if so, whether that loss is remediable. We review four bodies of evidence: the somatic marker framework, which positions emotion as an interoceptive process rather than an observable display; the debate between basic-emotion and constructionist accounts of facial expression, which bounds what external records can recover; the experiencing–remembering distinction and the peak-end literature, which show that retrospective evaluations diverge lawfully from concurrent ones; and the appraisal-based reconstruction of remembered emotion together with the accessibility model of self-report. Experience sampling is examined as a partial remedy. We conclude that emotional experience behaves as perishable data, with a validity window measured in hours, and that any preservation programme must be built around near-concurrent capture, preserved ambiguity, and the participant’s enduring control over sealing and deletion.

Keywords: emotional memory; somatic markers; constructed emotion; peak-end rule; experience sampling; cultural memory

1. Introduction

A record of an event is a physical object that survives the event and can be consulted later; an emotional experience is a process that terminates when it ceases to be felt. Photographs, video and diaries store records of the first kind with increasing fidelity and decreasing cost; nothing comparable exists for the second. The asymmetry is rarely noticed because records are assumed to carry emotional content implicitly. The cognitive science of emotion and memory gives three reasons to doubt this.

First, contemporary theories locate the core of emotional experience in interoceptive states not visible from the outside (Damasio, 1994, 1999; Barrett, 2017). Second, the mapping from visible expression to felt state is weaker and more context-dependent than early research supposed (Barrett et al., 2019). Third, the person’s own later account of an emotion is not a readout of a stored trace but a reconstruction shaped by current appraisals, current mood and semantic beliefs about the self (Levine, 1997; Levine & Safer, 2002; Robinson & Clore, 2002; Kahneman & Riis, 2005). Each literature is well developed; their joint implication for archival practice has, to our knowledge, not been drawn explicitly.

This article draws it. We argue that affective experience should be treated as perishable data: information whose validity decays rapidly after the moment of experience, such that records made later are records of something else. Sections 2 to 4 review the evidence, Section 5 evaluates experience sampling as a partial solution and situates the problem within the theory of cultural memory, and Section 6 derives requirements and ethical constraints for a preservation programme.

2. Emotion as an internal state

2.1 The somatic marker framework

Damasio’s (1994) somatic marker hypothesis arose from patients with ventromedial prefrontal damage who retained intact reasoning, language and factual memory while showing profound impairment in personal and social decision-making. The proposed mechanism is that bodily states elicited by past outcomes, or their centrally simulated equivalents, become associated with classes of situations and bias choice before deliberation is complete. The gambling task developed in Damasio’s laboratory, in which healthy participants showed anticipatory skin-conductance responses to disadvantageous decks before they could say why, provided the best-known support; its interpretation has since been contested, and the strong necessity claim remains debated. What has proved durable is the weaker claim sufficient here: the felt component of emotion is a change in the organism’s internal state, monitored interoceptively, and it does functional work.

Damasio (1999) further distinguished emotion, a patterned bodily response, from feeling, the organism’s representation of that response, and both from the extended consciousness in which feelings enter an autobiographical self. An observer with full access to the first level would still not possess the experience, which occurs at the second and third.

2.2 The constructionist reformulation

Barrett’s (2017) theory of constructed emotion agrees that the raw material of emotion is interoceptive but departs from Damasio on how that material becomes an instance of anger, joy or grief. The brain continuously predicts the body’s state and its likely causes; an emotion is a categorisation of interoceptive signals using concepts that are learned, culturally variable and applied in context. Two consequences follow: the interoceptive signal is not accessible to third parties, and the categorisation that makes it an emotion is an act of the experiencer that leaves no external residue unless reported.

On either account the conclusion for records is the same: the experience is not on the surface of the body, and the surface is what records capture.

3. What external records can and cannot capture

3.1 Basic emotions and the promise of the face

Ekman (1992) argued for a small set of basic emotions, each an evolved adaptation with a distinctive, universally recognisable facial signal and characteristic physiology. If that programme held in its strong form, a photograph would preserve the emotion category. Even then the record would be coarse: the signal is restricted to category membership and carries neither intensity, nor blends, nor the object of the emotion, nor the meaning the person assigned to it.

3.2 Reliability, specificity and generalisability

Barrett et al. (2019), reviewing the evidence in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, evaluated the strong programme against three criteria: whether a proposed configuration reliably occurs during the corresponding emotion, whether it is specific to that emotion, and whether the relation generalises across contexts and cultures. On all three, the evidence was judged insufficient. In the production studies reviewed, the configurations proposed for anger, sadness and other categories occurred in a minority of relevant episodes, and also during other states; perception studies inflate agreement through forced-choice formats. The authors do not claim that faces carry no information, only that it is probabilistic, context-bound and insufficient to infer a specific state from a facial configuration alone. Ekman and colleagues dispute the severity of this assessment. For archival purposes the point of contention is narrow: even the most favourable reading of the facial evidence yields a noisy category label, never the experience.

3.3 The diary and the delay

First-person records appear to escape the limitation because they contain the experiencer’s own words. Their weakness is temporal rather than perspectival: they are produced after the fact, and Section 4 shows that delay is not a neutral variable. Table 1 summarises the principal record types.

Record typePerspectiveDelayEmotion content preserved
Photograph / videoThird-personNoneProbabilistic category cue
Diary / letterFirst-personHours to daysReconstructed appraisal
Oral recollectionFirst-personYears to decadesSemantic self-belief; peak and end
Concurrent samplingFirst-personMinutesMomentary self-report

4. The reconstruction of remembered emotion

4.1 Experiencing and remembering

Kahneman and Riis (2005) distinguished the experiencing self, which registers hedonic states over a psychological present of a few seconds, from the remembering self, which evaluates episodes after they end. The remembering self is governed by a few representative moments rather than by the integral of experience over time. Redelmeier and Kahneman (1996) documented this in patients undergoing colonoscopy or lithotripsy, who rated pain at one-minute intervals and gave a global evaluation afterwards. Global evaluations were predicted by peak intensity and by intensity at the end of the procedure, and were largely insensitive to duration. The peak-end rule has been replicated across pleasant and unpleasant episodes. Every retrospective account of an emotional episode is thus generated by a system not designed to store the episode.

4.2 Memory for emotion is reconstructed from current appraisals

Levine (1997) tested the reconstruction hypothesis directly. Supporters of Ross Perot in the 1992 United States presidential election reported their emotions when Perot withdrew in July and, after he re-entered the race and the election concluded, recalled those initial feelings. Recalled sadness, anger and hope shifted towards participants’ current appraisals of Perot: those who remained loyal underestimated their earlier anger, whereas those who had abandoned him overestimated it. Levine and Safer (2002) identified three sources of bias in memory for emotion: current appraisals of the event, current emotional state, and coping processes that reduce the distress attached to past episodes. Intensity is typically overestimated in retrospect, and the direction of bias tracks present stance rather than original experience.

4.3 The accessibility model

Robinson and Clore (2002) offered a unifying account: emotional self-report draws on whichever source of information is most accessible at the time of reporting. During the experience, reports are anchored in experiential knowledge; shortly after, episodic memory provides partial access; as delay increases, reports are generated from semantic knowledge, that is, beliefs about oneself, about the type of situation, and about how people in general feel in such situations. Consistent with this, retrospective reports show effects of identity-related beliefs, including gender stereotypes about emotionality, that are absent from concurrent reports by the same individuals. The interval in which reports remain anchored in experience appears to be hours rather than days.

Together these literatures establish the central empirical claim of this paper. There is no stored trace of an emotional experience that later reports read out; reports are constructed from materials that are themselves changing, and become more semantic and self-serving with delay. After a brief window the experience has no reliable witness, including the person who had it.

5. Partial remedies and their limits

5.1 Experience sampling

The methodological response within psychology has been to move measurement into the window. The Experience Sampling Method (Csikszentmihalyi & Larson, 1987) uses random signals to prompt brief self-reports of activity, thought and affect several times a day over a week or more; its designers reported acceptable stability of aggregate affect measures, convergent validity, and modest reactivity. Ecological momentary assessment generalised the approach to clinical settings (Shiffman, Stone, & Hufford, 2008): momentary reports avoid recall bias, capture within-person variability that summary reports obliterate, and locate affect in context. The same review identified enduring limits: participant burden, non-random missing data, reactivity, and the reduction of experience to a few adjectives and scales.

Experience sampling shows that near-concurrent capture is feasible and yields data with different properties from recall. It does not solve the preservation problem, since it samples rather than records, describes populations rather than holding individuals’ experiences, and rarely retains its outputs beyond the study. It is nonetheless the closest existing paradigm to what a preservation programme would require.

5.2 The gap in cultural memory

The loss described above operates within the individual. Assmann (2011) describes its collective form. Communicative memory is carried in everyday interaction among contemporaries and extends over roughly three to four generations; cultural memory is fixed in texts, rites and institutions and can persist indefinitely. What crosses from the first to the second is what a society has formalised: names, dates, canonical narratives. What does not cross is the texture of lived experience, transmitted through tone, gesture and presence, which dies with its carriers. Emotional experience is therefore doubly perishable, within the individual over hours and within the group over generations, and no institution is charged with carrying it across either threshold.

6. Implications for emotion preservation

The evidence converts a vague intuition, that records miss something, into constraints that a programme for preserving emotional experience would have to satisfy, formulated here as requirements and testable propositions.

Requirement 1: capture must be near-concurrent. Sections 4.2 and 4.3 imply that the validity of a self-report as a record of experience declines with delay, steeply at first. Proposition 1a: for the same episode, reports collected within one hour will diverge measurably from reports collected after one week, and the divergence will be predicted by the participant’s current appraisal rather than by episode features. Proposition 1b: the divergence will be larger for negative and high-peak episodes.

Requirement 2: the record must preserve ambiguity. Sections 2 and 3 imply that forcing experience into a fixed category set, Ekman’s six or any other, discards what distinguishes experience from label. A record should allow mixed states, uncertainty and refusal to categorise. Proposition 2: participants given free or graded description will report blends and ambivalence at rates that forced-choice formats suppress.

Requirement 3: external records are auxiliary. Facial, vocal and contextual data have probabilistic value and should be stored as context, not as the emotion. Proposition 3: agreement between third-party inference from such records and concurrent self-report will remain modest (Barrett et al., 2019).

Requirement 4: the remembering self must be recorded too, separately. Later reconstructions are part of a person’s emotional history; concurrent reports and dated reappraisals should be retained without merging.

Requirement 5: the participant retains control over sealing and deletion. Levine and Safer (2002) identify coping-driven revision as a normal function of emotional memory; a perfect, permanently accessible archive would remove it. The right to be forgotten, articulated for digital records by Mayer-Schönberger (2009), applies with particular force to affective records and must extend to deferred access, sealing for a chosen period, and irreversible destruction at the participant’s request.

Requirement 6: consent must be revisited over time and must account for third parties. Emotions have objects, most of them other people. Consent given in the moment does not settle what a later self, or the persons implicated, would accept, and it is weakest where the case for preservation is strongest: in cognitive decline. Open questions include the sampling density that preserves individual trajectories, the reactivity cost of sustained self-observation, and whether a preserved experience can be transmitted to another person without becoming a record of the kind Section 3 describes.

7. Conclusion

The argument does not depend on resolving the disputes between Damasio and Barrett or between Ekman and his critics. On every account considered, emotional experience is internal, briefly accessible to its owner, and thereafter replaced by reconstructions that serve the present rather than the past. The archival technologies that have made external records nearly free have left the internal side of life as unrecorded as before. Treating affective experience as perishable data names the problem in a form that admits empirical work: a validity window, a decay function, capture conditions and rights. Whether the window can be used without distorting what passes through it is the central question for a preservation science.

Abstract

Consolidation theory long held that a memory trace, once stabilised by protein-synthesis-dependent processes, was resistant to disruption. The present review examines the evidence that retrieval returns consolidated memories to a labile state from which they must be restabilised (reconsolidation), and asks what this implies for the stability of emotional memories. We review the early demonstration by Misanin, Miller and Lewis (1968), the amygdala studies of Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000), the boundary conditions that determine whether reactivation destabilises a trace (reminder duration, trace age and strength, prediction error), and the human literature on pharmacological and behavioural interference with reconsolidation, including the contested replication record of the reactivation–extinction procedure. We then situate reconsolidation within the constructive-memory tradition of Bartlett, Loftus and Schacter. The main conclusion is that emotional memories are neither fixed records nor freely rewritable: they are updated under specific, partly characterised conditions, most reliably when retrieval carries a prediction error. For a programme aiming to preserve emotional memory, any elicitation of a memory is potentially an intervention on it, and preservation must be conceived as the documentation of dated reconstructions rather than the retrieval of an original.

Keywords: reconsolidation; constructive memory; fear conditioning; prediction error; propranolol; misinformation effect

1. Introduction

The standard model of memory formation distinguishes a brief post-encoding period during which a trace is vulnerable from a subsequent state in which it is stable. During the vulnerable period, amnesic agents such as electroconvulsive shock or protein-synthesis inhibitors abolish the memory; afterwards they are without effect. The implicit corollary of this consolidation hypothesis was that consolidation happens once: a trace was not thought to re-enter a state of vulnerability simply because it had been retrieved.

Two lines of research have challenged this corollary from opposite directions. The first, neurobiological, is the reconsolidation literature: animal and human work showing that retrieval can render a consolidated memory transiently labile, such that amnesic agents administered after reactivation impair subsequent expression. The second, psychological, is the constructive-memory tradition, which since Bartlett (1932) has documented that remembering is reconstructive, shaped by schemas, post-event information and current goals. These literatures converge on a single claim: the act of remembering is not neutral with respect to the memory remembered.

The present review summarises the reconsolidation evidence with attention to its boundary conditions, since the popular reading that every recall rewrites the past overstates what has been shown; assesses the human literature, where translational promise has been tempered by a mixed replication record; and draws out the implications for efforts to preserve emotional memories.

2. From consolidation to reconsolidation

2.1 Early evidence and its neglect

The first clear demonstration that a consolidated memory could be made vulnerable by reactivation is attributed to Misanin, Miller and Lewis (1968). Twenty-four hours after rats received a single tone–footshock pairing, beyond the consolidation window as then understood, one group was re-exposed to the tone and then given electroconvulsive shock; a second group received the shock without re-exposure. Only the reactivated group showed retrograde amnesia. The finding was replicated during the 1970s but was widely treated as a curiosity and largely set aside for three decades (Dudai, 2012).

2.2 Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000)

The modern literature dates from Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000). Rats were trained on auditory fear conditioning, in which freezing to a shock-paired tone indexes the memory. One day after training, the tone was presented once without shock, and the protein-synthesis inhibitor anisomycin was infused into the lateral and basal amygdala immediately afterwards. Animals tested the following day showed markedly reduced freezing relative to vehicle-infused controls, whereas anisomycin without reactivation, and reactivation without anisomycin, left the memory intact. The same result held for fourteen-day-old memories, ruling out a merely extended consolidation window. The authors concluded that retrieval returns the trace to a labile state and that restabilisation, or reconsolidation, requires new protein synthesis. The design logic underlies every subsequent study: reconsolidation is inferred from an interaction in which an amnesic manipulation impairs the memory only when combined with prior reactivation.

2.3 Dudai’s synthesis

Dudai’s reviews (2004, 2012) provided the conceptual framework in which these findings are discussed. He distinguished synaptic consolidation, over hours and dependent on local protein synthesis, from systems consolidation, over weeks to years and involving circuit reorganisation. Reconsolidation re-engages synaptic consolidation after reactivation, and its function is proposed to be adaptive: it permits an existing trace to be updated with information available at retrieval. Dudai (2012) was explicit that this reading remains a hypothesis: post-reactivation vulnerability is well established in several species, but the claim that the labile period exists to permit updating is an inference from it.

3. Boundary conditions

If every retrieval destabilised every memory, far more forgetting and distortion would be observed than is. The effect is gated by several conditions, and characterising them has been the principal work of the past two decades (Lee, Nader & Schiller, 2017).

3.1 Reminder duration

Pedreira and Maldonado (2003), working with the crab Chasmagnathus, showed that reminder duration determines which process is engaged. A brief re-exposure to the training context destabilised the memory, so that a protein-synthesis inhibitor produced amnesia; a prolonged re-exposure produced extinction, which the same inhibitor now blocked while leaving the original memory intact. Reconsolidation and extinction are thus alternative outcomes of reactivation, with the boundary set by the amount of non-reinforced exposure. The reminder must be long enough to destabilise the trace but not so long as to initiate extinction, and the optimal parameters are not known a priori.

3.2 Trace age and strength

In rodents, memories that are weeks old or overtrained often fail to show post-reactivation vulnerability under reminder conditions sufficient for younger or weaker memories, although more discrepant reminders can sometimes restore it (Lee et al., 2017). The generality of this constraint in humans is uncertain, since most human studies use memories that are one day old.

3.3 Prediction error

The most theoretically productive boundary condition is prediction error. Sevenster, Beckers and Kindt (2013) trained participants on differential fear conditioning and administered propranolol after a reactivation trial. When the reactivation trial was arranged so that its outcome was fully predicted, propranolol had no effect on later fear-potentiated startle; when reactivation involved a violation of expectancy, propranolol abolished the startle response. Retrieval alone is therefore not sufficient: current input must diverge from what the trace predicts. This is consistent with Dudai’s functional hypothesis, since a memory is opened for revision precisely when there is something to revise, and it constrains applications, because the same reminder can produce a prediction error for one individual and none for another.
