4. Reconsolidation in humans

4.1 Pharmacological interference

Kindt, Soeter and Vervliet (2009) provided the first widely cited human demonstration. After differential fear conditioning, one group received oral propranolol, a β-adrenergic antagonist, before a single unreinforced presentation of the conditioned stimulus on the following day. On the third day, fear-potentiated startle was abolished in this group but not in placebo or no-reactivation controls, and did not return after reinstatement shocks. Declarative knowledge of the contingency, indexed by expectancy ratings, was unaffected. Whether this constitutes erasure of an amygdala-dependent component or a change in its expression remains debated (Lee et al., 2017), but the dissociation between affective expression and declarative content has been replicated within the same laboratory.

4.2 Behavioural updating and its replication record

Schiller et al. (2010) asked whether the reconsolidation window could be exploited without drugs. After fear conditioning, participants received a single reminder trial and then underwent extinction either ten minutes later, within the putative window, or six hours later, outside it. Return of skin-conductance responses on the third day was absent only in the ten-minute group, and a subset showed no return of fear approximately one year later. Extinction inside the window was interpreted as updating the fear memory itself, rather than forming a separate inhibitory trace.

The replication record of this reactivation–extinction effect is mixed, and the present review regards it as contested. Some laboratories reported conceptual replications; others failed to observe the effect with startle or skin conductance (Lee et al., 2017). Chalkia et al. (2020) conducted a registered, high-powered direct replication of the original design and found no persistent attenuation of fear in the ten-minute group, with return of fear across all conditions. They concluded not that reconsolidation does not occur in humans, but that the procedure as described does not reliably produce it. The most parsimonious reading is that behavioural updating is possible but sensitive to parameters not yet controlled, plausibly including whether the reminder generates a prediction error (Sevenster et al., 2013).

4.3 Episodic memory

Hupbach, Gomez, Hardt and Nadel (2007) extended the logic to episodic memory. Participants learned a list of objects on day one. On day two, one group received a subtle reminder (the same experimenter, the same room and a question about the original session) before learning a second list; another group learned it without the reminder. On day three, recall of the first list showed substantial, asymmetric intrusions from the second list only in the reminded group, as a reconsolidation account predicts. The phenomenon is thus not confined to amygdala-dependent aversive learning.

5. Constructive memory: the psychological tradition

5.1 Bartlett

Bartlett (1932) asked participants to reproduce an unfamiliar folk narrative, “The War of the Ghosts”, at intervals over weeks and months. Successive reproductions became shorter, more coherent by the participants’ cultural standards, and populated with details absent from the original. He concluded that remembering is a reconstruction from fragments guided by schemas rather than the re-reading of a stored record. His methods were informal by contemporary standards, but the central claim has survived a century of testing.

5.2 Loftus and the misinformation effect

Loftus (2005) reviewed three decades of research on the misinformation effect, in which post-event information alters subsequent recall. A reliable proportion of participants exposed to misleading post-event information incorporate it into their reports. Loftus also reviewed studies in which fictitious childhood events, such as being lost in a shopping mall, were implanted through suggestion in roughly a quarter of participants. The paradigm structurally resembles the reconsolidation designs reviewed above: a memory is reactivated, new information follows, and that information is later reported as part of the original. It would be premature to assert that misinformation effects are mediated by synaptic reconsolidation, but the convergence with Hupbach et al. (2007) is at minimum suggestive.

5.3 Schacter’s adaptive account

Schacter (1999) organised memory failures into seven categories: sins of omission (transience, absent-mindedness, blocking), sins of commission (misattribution, suggestibility, bias) and persistence, the unwanted recurrence of distressing memories. His argument, developed in Schacter (2012), is that these failures are by-products of processes that are adaptive on the whole: a system that extracts gist, integrates new information and simulates future events will necessarily be prone to distortion. On this view, reconsolidation is a candidate mechanism through which such constructive processes are implemented, although the neurobiological and functional accounts are argued at different levels and neither is fully specified.

6. Implications for emotion preservation

The literature reviewed yields several constraints on any programme that aims to preserve human emotional memory. We formulate them as testable propositions.

First, there is no stable original to be retrieved. An emotional memory retrieved and reconsolidated many times is the product of that history, and its current form cannot be distinguished, from the inside, from earlier forms. Preservation should therefore be conceived as the documentation of dated reconstructions. A record of a grief one month after loss and a record of the same grief ten years later are different objects, and a programme that treats them as interchangeable misdescribes both.

Second, elicitation is intervention. Any procedure that asks a person to retrieve an emotional memory in order to document it reactivates the trace and, under some conditions, destabilises it. Those conditions include a brief reminder and, most reliably, a prediction error. Elicitation contexts that are novel, ask unexpected questions, or confront the person with discrepant information are the ones most likely to modify what they aim to record. This is testable: memories elicited under high-discrepancy conditions should show greater change on subsequent elicitation than memories elicited under low-discrepancy conditions.

Third, emotional and declarative components may dissociate. The propranolol studies show that affective expression can be attenuated while declarative content is spared. A programme that documents only declarative content risks preserving a description of an emotion rather than the emotion; one that documents only physiological markers risks a response detached from its object.

Fourth, the replication record counsels modesty. Human reconsolidation research has established that updating is possible but not that it is reliable, and the boundary conditions are less well characterised in humans than in rodents. Preservation practices should measure change rather than presume its absence; current evidence requires caution but does not specify safe procedures.

7. Conclusion

Reconsolidation research has replaced a model in which consolidation happens once with one in which retrieval can, under specific conditions, reopen a trace for revision. The evidence for post-reactivation vulnerability is strong in animals and reasonably strong for pharmacological interference in humans; the evidence for behavioural updating in humans is contested, and prediction error emerges as the most consistent gating factor. Read alongside the constructive-memory tradition, these findings support a view of emotional memory as a maintained reconstruction rather than a stored record. That view does not make emotional memories arbitrary; it makes them historical, and places the act of remembering, including remembering for preservation, among the forces that shape what is remembered.

Abstract

Emotionally arousing experiences are remembered longer and more vividly than neutral ones, yet vividness is a poor guide to accuracy. This review examines the mechanisms behind both facts. The modulation hypothesis (McGaugh, 2004, 2015) holds that peripheral stress hormones, acting through noradrenergic signalling in the basolateral amygdala, strengthen consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories; β-adrenergic blockade in humans abolishes the emotional memory advantage (Cahill et al., 1994), and amygdala–medial temporal lobe coupling at encoding predicts later retention (Dolcos et al., 2004). Behavioural research qualifies this picture: arousal biases competition toward high-priority elements (Mather & Sutherland, 2011), negative valence preserves item detail at the expense of context (Kensinger, 2009), and amygdala-dependent emotional binding decays more slowly than hippocampal contextual binding (Yonelinas & Ritchey, 2015). Longitudinal studies of flashbulb memories show that consistency declines at ordinary rates while confidence remains elevated (Talarico & Rubin, 2003; Hirst et al., 2015). We conclude that emotion regulates the strength and selectivity of a memory trace, not its fidelity, and that a programme for preserving emotional memory must record the temporal dynamics of the trace rather than a single retrospective account.

Keywords: emotional memory; consolidation; amygdala; flashbulb memories; arousal-biased competition; metamemory

1. Introduction

Two observations about emotional memory are well established and, at first sight, difficult to reconcile. Experiences accompanied by emotional arousal are retained better and for longer than comparable neutral experiences, an effect documented across species, paradigms and delays. Yet the vividness of such memories is only weakly related to their accuracy: people reporting exceptionally clear recollections of consequential public events are frequently inconsistent with their own earlier reports, with no corresponding loss of confidence.

The present review argues that the two findings follow from a single principle. Emotion does not act as a recording device with a higher resolution setting; it acts as a modulator that adjusts the strength with which a trace is consolidated and biases which components of an experience receive that benefit. Because the modulatory signal is indexed to arousal rather than to informational content, it enhances retention and subjective certainty without verifying what is retained. Sections 2 to 4 review the neurobiology of modulated consolidation, the selectivity of emotional enhancement, and the dissociation between vividness and accuracy in flashbulb and eyewitness memory; Section 5 draws out constraints for a programme of preserving human emotional memory.

2. Hormonal and amygdalar modulation of consolidation

2.1 The modulation hypothesis

Memory traces stabilise over hours to days after encoding, and McGaugh’s modulation hypothesis holds that this consolidation window is where emotional arousal exerts its principal influence (McGaugh, 2004, 2015). The rodent evidence rests on post-training manipulations: adrenaline or glucocorticoids administered shortly after learning enhance later retention, whereas the same treatments given several hours later do not. Because the manipulation follows learning, the effect cannot reflect altered attention during the event; it is dose-dependent and follows an inverted-U function.

Adrenaline does not readily cross the blood–brain barrier; its effects are mediated through vagal afferents to the nucleus of the solitary tract, which projects to the locus coeruleus and thereby increases noradrenaline release in the basolateral amygdala (BLA). BLA lesions, or intra-BLA β-adrenergic antagonists, block the memory-enhancing effects of systemic adrenaline and glucocorticoids, whereas intra-BLA noradrenergic agonists enhance retention. Critically, the BLA is not the storage site of the memories it modulates: its influence is exerted on the hippocampus, caudate and cortical regions, and BLA lesions abolish only the arousal-dependent increment in retention, not learning itself (McGaugh, 2004). Glucocorticoid enhancement likewise requires intact β-adrenergic signalling within the BLA (McGaugh, 2015).

2.2 Causal evidence in humans

The translation of this model to humans was provided by Cahill et al. (1994). Participants viewed a slide sequence accompanied by either a neutral narrative or an arousing narrative whose central phase described a boy’s serious injury and surgery, having received 40 mg of the β-adrenergic antagonist propranolol or placebo one hour earlier. At a surprise test one week later, placebo participants showed enhanced recall and recognition for the arousing phase relative to the neutral story; in the propranolol group this enhancement was absent, whereas memory for the neutral story was unaffected. Propranolol thus selectively removed the arousal-dependent increment rather than producing a general impairment, as the modulation hypothesis predicts. Cahill and McGaugh (1998) integrated this with evidence from patients with amygdala damage, who lack the normal enhancement for arousing narrative material, and with early imaging data in which amygdala activity at encoding predicted later recall of emotional but not neutral films, into an account in which the amygdala modulates lasting declarative memory in proportion to peripheral adrenergic activation.

2.3 Amygdala circuits and amygdala–hippocampal interaction

The circuitry through which the amygdala detects emotional significance has been characterised most thoroughly in Pavlovian fear conditioning (LeDoux, 2000). Sensory information reaches the lateral nucleus of the amygdala by a direct thalamic projection that is fast but coarse and by a longer thalamo-cortical route that supplies a more processed representation; output through the central nucleus recruits autonomic, endocrine and behavioural responses. LeDoux (2000) distinguished this implicit emotional memory, expressed as a conditioned response, from hippocampus-dependent declarative memory of the same episode. The two dissociate: patients with selective amygdala damage retain declarative knowledge that a stimulus predicted shock but show no conditioned autonomic response, whereas patients with selective hippocampal damage show the reverse (Phelps & LeDoux, 2005).

In the intact human brain the systems interact. Phelps (2004) described two complementary influences: the amygdala enhances hippocampal encoding and consolidation of arousing events, and the hippocampus supplies contextual representations that allow fear responses to be acquired by instruction and modified by context; the amygdala’s modulatory reach also extends to attention and perception (Phelps & LeDoux, 2005). The most direct imaging evidence for the encoding-stage interaction comes from Dolcos, LaBar and Cabeza (2004), who used a subsequent-memory design with emotional and neutral pictures. Activity in the amygdala, hippocampus and entorhinal cortex was greater for pictures later remembered than for those forgotten, more so for emotional pictures, and amygdala activity correlated more strongly with medial temporal lobe activity for emotional than for neutral items, consistent with a modulatory interaction rather than two independent contributions.

3. The selectivity of emotional enhancement

3.1 Arousal-biased competition

The consolidation account explains why arousing memories persist, but not why they are detailed in some respects and impoverished in others. Under the arousal-biased competition model of Mather and Sutherland (2011), arousal amplifies existing differences in priority: representations already winning the competition for processing resources, through bottom-up salience or top-down goal relevance, gain further from arousal, whereas low-priority representations lose. The model accounts for findings that arousal improves memory for a target while impairing memory for a concurrent low-priority stimulus, and predicts that the direction of the effect for any element depends on its priority at encoding rather than its emotional content as such. Emotion increases the contrast within a memory rather than its overall resolution.

3.2 Valence, detail and the trade-off between item and context

Kensinger (2009) reviewed evidence that valence and arousal have partly separable effects on memory content. Negative arousing items tend to be remembered with greater intrinsic detail, such as exact visual form, whereas positive items are more often remembered as gist and are more susceptible to misattribution. Emotional items are also frequently associated with poorer memory for the neutral background against which they appeared, the memory trade-off. Kensinger attributed the negative-valence advantage to greater sensory engagement at encoding and noted that it is item-focused, not extending to associative or contextual features. A negative emotional memory may therefore be more accurate for its focal object and less accurate for the surrounding circumstances than a neutral memory of comparable age.

3.3 Emotional binding and slow forgetting

Yonelinas and Ritchey (2015) addressed the temporal profile of these effects. Reviewing studies with delays from minutes to days, they observed that emotional items are not merely better remembered at a given delay but are forgotten more slowly than neutral items, with the advantage expressed mainly in recollection rather than familiarity. Their emotional binding account proposes that the amygdala supports binding of an item to its emotional significance, an association relatively resistant to interference and decay, whereas the hippocampus supports binding of the item to its episodic context, which decays more rapidly. Emotion thus preserves memory for the item and its affective quality while contextual details follow an ordinary forgetting curve, which supplies a mechanism for Kensinger’s trade-off: the amygdala-dependent trace outlasts the hippocampal contextual trace, leaving a strongly felt memory of a central element with degraded surroundings.

4. Vividness without fidelity

4.1 Flashbulb memories

Brown and Kulik (1977) introduced the term flashbulb memory for the detailed recollection of the circumstances in which one learned of a surprising and consequential public event, drawing on retrospective reports of the Kennedy assassination, and proposed a dedicated “Now Print!” mechanism. Their design could not assess accuracy, however, because no baseline account existed for comparison.

Test–retest designs address this limitation. Talarico and Rubin (2003) collected reports from 54 undergraduates on 12 September 2001 concerning both how they learned of the attacks and an ordinary recent event, then retested subgroups after 1, 6 or 32 weeks. Consistency with the initial report declined at similar rates for both memories, but ratings of vividness, belief in accuracy and reliving remained high for the flashbulb memory while declining for the everyday memory. A much larger multi-site study (Hirst et al., 2015) followed the same logic over a decade. Participants were surveyed within days of the attacks and again at approximately 11 months, 35 months and 119 months. Consistency of flashbulb memories fell sharply within the first year and then stabilised, with early inconsistencies tending to persist rather than to be corrected; memory for facts about the event showed a similar profile. Throughout, confidence remained high and was only weakly related to consistency. Neither study supports a mechanism that guarantees accuracy; both indicate that emotional significance sustains the experience of remembering after the content has drifted.

4.2 Weapon focus

The dissociation is visible at a shorter time scale in eyewitness paradigms. Loftus, Loftus and Messo (1987) presented slide sequences of a customer in a fast-food restaurant who either handed the cashier a cheque or pointed a gun. Participants made more and longer eye fixations on the gun than on the cheque, and memory for other details, including identification of the customer, was poorer in the weapon condition. The pattern matches arousal-biased competition: the high-priority weapon captures attention and is well encoded while the rest of the scene suffers. Laboratory effect sizes are moderate, the relative contributions of arousal and of a weapon’s unusualness are debated, and field studies are mixed; what the paradigm shows unambiguously is that an arousing object redistributes encoding, so that a witness can be accurate and confident about the weapon while inaccurate about the perpetrator.

4.3 A common interpretation

These literatures support a single interpretation. The arousal signal that enhances consolidation is generated by the emotional response, not by any assessment of the accuracy of what is encoded. It strengthens whatever was prioritised at the time and attaches an affective tag that persists after contextual detail has decayed. At retrieval, the persistence of that tag and of the item it marks produces a strong sense of recollection that is experienced as evidence of fidelity, while reconstruction of the degraded periphery draws on general knowledge, later conversation and media exposure and inherits the confidence associated with the core. Vividness and confidence are thus readouts of modulatory strength, whereas accuracy is a property of content that emotion neither measures nor protects.

5. Implications for emotion preservation

A programme aimed at preserving human emotional memory must be designed around the properties reviewed here, several of which can be stated as requirements or testable propositions.

First, the trace of an emotional experience is not stable when formed. Arousal exerts its strongest effect during the consolidation window of hours to days, and contextual consistency declines most steeply during the first year (Hirst et al., 2015). A preservation protocol should therefore obtain an account as close as possible to the event and at least one further account after consolidation, treating the pair as jointly constitutive of the memory rather than selecting one as canonical. Because early inconsistencies persist rather than self-correct, a delayed first record cannot be repaired by later collection.

Second, the components of an emotional memory decay at different rates. Affective significance and the focal item are expected to persist; peripheral context is expected to follow ordinary forgetting. A record should distinguish these components explicitly and should not treat the completeness of a retrospective narrative as a proxy for accuracy. It is a testable prediction that measures of affective binding, such as ratings of feeling and item recognition, will remain stable across years whereas contextual detail will not, and preservation quality should be assessed against this expected profile rather than against an ideal of total recall.

Third, confidence, vividness and the sense of reliving are properties of the emotional trace in their own right and should be recorded as data, not used as validation. The dissociation between confidence and consistency implies that self-reported certainty is uninformative about accuracy and informative about modulatory strength.

Fourth, since arousal biases encoding toward prioritised elements, what a person selectively retained is itself a record of what mattered to them. Whether to supplement the selective trace with external contextual records or to preserve the selection as lived is an open question; the two aims are not interchangeable and their relative value for the person should be studied empirically.

6. Conclusion

The evidence reviewed converges on an account in which emotion operates on memory as a modulator rather than a recorder. Peripheral adrenergic and glucocorticoid signals, relayed through the basolateral amygdala, strengthen consolidation of hippocampus-dependent traces, an effect demonstrated causally in humans by pharmacological blockade. The enhancement is selective, favouring prioritised and negatively valenced items over context, and durable, with amygdala-dependent binding outlasting hippocampal contextual binding. The same mechanism that produces persistence produces confidence, which is why vivid recollections of consequential events remain compelling while their content drifts. Emotional memory is well adapted for retaining what mattered and guiding future behaviour; it is not adapted for archival fidelity, and research and practice should proceed from that distinction.

body:
Abstract

Forgetting is commonly treated as a failure of the memory system, a passive loss of information through decay or interference. The present review examines the alternative position that forgetting is, in substantial part, adaptive and often active. Four bodies of evidence are considered: the classical retention data of Ebbinghaus and their reinterpretation in the new theory of disuse; behavioural work on retrieval-induced forgetting and on the deliberate suppression of unwanted memories, together with its neural correlates; recent neurobiological accounts of intrinsic forgetting mechanisms, including synaptic weakening and hippocampal neurogenesis; and the study of individuals with exceptional retention, from Luria’s mnemonist to highly superior autobiographical memory. Across these literatures, forgetting emerges as a set of mechanisms that reduce interference, support generalisation and permit behavioural updating in changing environments, although the replication status and boundary conditions of some effects remain contested. The main conclusion is that a memory system without forgetting would be neither more accurate nor more useful. For any programme that seeks to preserve human emotional memory, this implies that fidelity should be defined by the functional role of a memory rather than by the completeness of its record.

Keywords: forgetting; retrieval-induced forgetting; memory suppression; inhibition; neurogenesis; hyperthymesia

1. Introduction

The everyday model of memory is a storage model: experiences are deposited, retained and later withdrawn, and any discrepancy between the two counts as loss. Within this model forgetting has no function, and the ideal system is one that never forgets.

This model has been challenged from several directions. Theoretical work reframed the loss of accessibility as a precondition for efficient learning (Bjork & Bjork, 1992). Experimental work showed that forgetting can be produced by the act of remembering itself (Anderson, Bjork, & Bjork, 1994) and by deliberate cognitive control (Anderson & Green, 2001), with identifiable prefrontal and hippocampal correlates (Anderson & Hanslmayr, 2014). Neurobiological reviews have catalogued molecular and cellular processes whose apparent purpose is to remove stored traces (Davis & Zhong, 2017; Richards & Frankland, 2017). Case studies of exceptional retainers reveal costs rather than unqualified benefits (LePort et al., 2012; Luria, 1968; Parker, Cahill, & McGaugh, 2006). Nørby (2015) has offered the most systematic functional taxonomy of these findings.

The present review has two aims: to assess how strong the evidence is that forgetting is adaptive and, where relevant, active rather than passive, distinguishing established from contested findings; and to derive constraints for any effort to preserve human emotional memory, a domain in which the equation of fidelity with completeness is particularly seductive and, we argue, misleading.

2. Classical retention data and the theory of disuse

2.1 Ebbinghaus and the savings method

The quantitative study of forgetting begins with Ebbinghaus (1885/1913), who learned lists of nonsense syllables to criterion and measured retention by the savings method: the reduction in trials needed to relearn a list relative to original learning, at intervals from about twenty minutes to thirty-one days. The resulting function is steep at first and then flattens, so that most measurable loss occurs within the first day. Two features are often neglected. First, savings remained positive at the longest intervals even when unaided recall was at floor: a trace can persist without being accessible. Second, repetitions distributed over days produced markedly better retention than the same number massed within a session. The data rest on a single participant, but the shape of the function has been replicated many times, and the dissociation between availability and accessibility became a cornerstone of later theory.

2.2 Storage strength and retrieval strength

Bjork and Bjork (1992) formalised this dissociation in the new theory of disuse. Each memory carries two independent indices: storage strength, which reflects how well an item is learned and interconnected and is assumed never to decrease, and retrieval strength, which reflects current accessibility and is what declines with disuse and competition. Retrieval strength is a limited resource, so that gains for some items entail losses for others; increments to storage strength are larger when retrieval strength is low; and retrieval is a more potent learning event than re-study.

Under these assumptions the loss of retrieval strength is not a defect but the condition that makes subsequent learning efficient while keeping older information available. The theory accounts for the spacing effect and for the advantage of testing over restudy, and it predicts that forgetting should be selective and use-dependent, because retrieval strength is redistributed according to what the organism actually retrieves.

3. Forgetting produced by remembering

3.1 Retrieval-induced forgetting

Anderson, Bjork, and Bjork (1994) introduced the retrieval-practice paradigm. Participants study category–exemplar pairs (Fruit–Orange, Fruit–Banana, Drink–Whisky), then practise retrieving half of the exemplars from half of the categories using stem cues (*Fruit–Or___). The critical comparison at final test is between unpractised items from practised categories (Banana) and items from unpractised categories (Whisky): the former were recalled less well, an effect termed retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF). The authors’ interpretation was inhibitory: when Fruit* cues retrieval of Orange, competing fruits are activated and must be suppressed, and this suppression persists as reduced accessibility.

Two findings were subsequently taken to favour inhibition over associative blocking, on which practised items simply become stronger competitors at test: RIF appears with independent cues absent during practice, and it depends on retrieval practice rather than on extra study of the same items. Both have been replicated, but neither is uncontested.

3.2 Replication and moderators

In the meta-analysis by Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli, and Storm (2014), RIF was reliable and of moderate size, and its magnitude was moderated by the integration of materials, the strength of competitors and the delay between practice and test. Some moderator patterns are consistent with inhibition and some equally with interference-based accounts. RIF is therefore a robust behavioural phenomenon whose mechanism remains debated; claims that hinge specifically on inhibition should be presented as provisional.

3.3 Deliberate suppression: the think/no-think paradigm

Anderson and Green (2001) asked whether forgetting could be produced intentionally. In the think/no-think (TNT) paradigm, participants learn weakly related word pairs (Ordeal–Roach). Cues are then presented repeatedly; for Think items participants recall the response, whereas for No-Think items they prevent the response from entering awareness. At the final test, recall of No-Think items fell below that of baseline items learned but not presented in the second phase, and the deficit increased with the number of suppression trials (0, 1, 8 and 16). The deficit was also observed with independent probes, which argues against participants merely associating the cue with something else.

The TNT effect has been replicated in many laboratories, although it is modest, a proportion of participants show no effect, and null results have been reported, particularly when compliance is not enforced. Individual differences correlate with executive control, and reduced effects have been reported in post-traumatic stress and depression, although these associations rest on small samples.

3.4 Neural mechanisms of motivated forgetting

Anderson and Hanslmayr (2014) reviewed the neuroimaging and electrophysiological evidence and distinguished two mechanisms. Direct suppression engages right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during No-Think trials and reduces hippocampal activity, and the degree of both predicts later forgetting. Thought substitution recruits left ventrolateral prefrontal regions associated with selective retrieval. The direct-suppression network overlaps with that implicated in stopping motor responses, suggesting that memory suppression is one application of a domain-general inhibitory control system. The causal role of hippocampal downregulation, however, has been established mainly by correlation with subsequent recall.

4. The biology of active forgetting

The behavioural literature establishes that forgetting can be selective and controllable, not that the brain is built to forget. Richards and Frankland (2017) distinguish persistence, the mechanisms that stabilise engrams, from transience, the mechanisms that degrade them, and argue that both are regulated. Evidence for active transience includes activity-dependent weakening of synaptic connections, loss of dendritic spines, and adult hippocampal neurogenesis: newly integrated neurons remodel existing circuits, and in rodents increasing neurogenesis after learning accelerates forgetting whereas suppressing it slows forgetting. Their functional argument is drawn from machine learning: a learner that stores every training example overfits, whereas transience discards idiosyncratic detail, promotes generalisation and, in non-stationary environments, removes information that has become misleading. On this view the goal of memory is adaptive decision-making in the present rather than accurate transmission of the past.

Davis and Zhong (2017) reach a parallel conclusion from molecular data, largely from Drosophila. They argue that the default state of newly formed memories is to be forgotten, through an intrinsic pathway in which the small GTPase Rac1 and cytoskeletal remodelling erode labile traces and dopaminergic signalling after learning drives ongoing forgetting. Blocking these pathways prolongs memory; activating them accelerates its loss. Generalisation from invertebrate conditioning to human autobiographical memory must be cautious. What the two reviews jointly establish is that some forgetting is the product of dedicated biological machinery rather than entropy: a process the organism pays for presumably yields a return.

5. The costs of exceptional retention

If forgetting is functional, individuals who forget less should exhibit the costs of its absence. The evidence is case-based and cannot support causal inference, but it is consistent in direction.

Luria (1968) followed the mnemonist S. for nearly thirty years. S. reproduced lists of seventy or more items in any order and recalled lists learned fifteen years earlier, relying on pronounced synaesthesia and an involuntary conversion of words into images. Luria’s clinical observations concern the costs. S. had difficulty extracting the gist of a text because each word generated an image that competed with the next; he found metaphor hard to process; he had difficulty recognising faces, because each instance had been stored separately; and material from previous performances intruded on later ones. Its central observation, that indiscriminate retention interferes with abstraction, anticipates the overfitting argument above.

Parker, Cahill, and McGaugh (2006) reported the case of AJ, who could recall the events of nearly any day of her adult life when given a date, verified against diaries; her performance on many standard laboratory tests was unremarkable, and her recall was described as automatic, uncontrollable and at times burdensome. LePort et al. (2012) studied eleven individuals with highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) against matched controls. HSAM participants were dramatically superior on tests of public and personal event memory, yet performed at control levels on most standard laboratory measures. Structural imaging revealed differences in temporal and parietal regions, and HSAM participants scored higher on measures of obsessional tendencies. Subsequent work has found HSAM individuals as susceptible as controls to laboratory-induced false memories. The literature is small, but it demonstrates that superior retention does not generalise to superior cognition and carries a distinctive profile of costs.

Nørby (2015) organises these findings into three adaptive functions: emotional regulation, as the affective charge of negative experiences attenuates; cognitive economy, as competing information that retrieval must search is reduced; and knowledge acquisition, as episodes are abstracted into schemas. These functions can conflict with one another and with accuracy, so the value of forgetting is contingent rather than absolute. The taxonomy clarifies where forgetting becomes pathological: not when much is lost, but when what is lost is required for the functions that remain.

6. Implications for emotion preservation

The findings reviewed impose constraints on any programme for preserving human emotional memory, stated here as propositions open to empirical test.

First, the fidelity of an emotional memory cannot be defined by the completeness of its record. An affective trace that persists across a lifetime has been shaped by transience: peripheral detail has been discarded and the residual tone, evaluation and relational meaning have been abstracted (Nørby, 2015; Richards & Frankland, 2017). The testable proposition is that judgements of authenticity by the rememberer will track the abstracted form of an emotional memory more closely than its detailed original.

Second, accessibility and availability are distinct (Bjork & Bjork, 1992; Ebbinghaus, 1885/1913). A programme may aim to preserve availability while leaving accessibility to the person’s own retrieval history. The proposition is that re-exposed material will be experienced as more intrusive, and less as one’s own, when it restores accessibility the individual has allowed to lapse.

Third, the capacity to suppress is a competence with a neural basis and clinical significance (Anderson & Green, 2001; Anderson & Hanslmayr, 2014). Material the individual has deliberately kept from awareness should not be reinstated without consent, and any protocol should be evaluated for its effects on intrusion frequency in vulnerable groups.

Fourth, retrieval strengthens what is retrieved and impairs what is not (Anderson et al., 1994; Murayama et al., 2014). Repeated cued recall of selected emotional episodes will strengthen them at the expense of related unrehearsed ones; selection criteria are therefore an intervention on the memory system, and their effects on the unselected remainder should be measured.

Fifth, the HSAM and mnemonist data (LePort et al., 2012; Luria, 1968; Parker et al., 2006) caution that an exhaustive emotional archive is not a model of psychological health. Which features of an emotional memory carry its long-term function is an open question that should precede decisions about what to retain.

7. Conclusion

The evidence reviewed converges on a position stronger than the claim that forgetting is tolerable: at least some forgetting is produced by mechanisms the organism maintains at a cost, is regulated by the same control systems that govern action, and yields benefits in generalisation, updating and affective regulation that a non-forgetting system would lack. The position has limits: the inhibitory interpretation of retrieval-induced forgetting is contested, suppression effects are modest and variable, and the molecular evidence comes largely from invertebrates. What is not in doubt is that the exceptional retainers studied to date do not think better for retaining more. Programmes concerned with emotional memory should begin from the functions that forgetting serves, not from the assumption that the best memory loses nothing.

title: The Architecture of Autobiographical Memory: Hierarchical Organisation and Sources of Fragility
description: Autobiographical memory is often treated as a store of discrete personal episodes that can be retrieved and copied. This review examines whether the evidence supports that assumption. We consider the hierarchical self-memory system of Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000),…
body:
Abstract

Autobiographical memory is often treated as a store of discrete personal episodes that can be retrieved and copied. This review examines whether the evidence supports that assumption. We consider the hierarchical self-memory system of Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000), Tulving’s distinction between episodic and semantic memory and his account of autonoetic consciousness, Rubin’s basic-systems model, and the reconstructive tradition initiated by Bartlett (1932). We then review neural evidence from neuroimaging meta-analyses and behavioural evidence from the Autobiographical Interview, lifespan studies of episodic and semantic autobiographical recall, childhood amnesia and the reminiscence bump. The convergent conclusion is that a personal memory is a transient construction assembled across several levels of knowledge and several neurocognitive systems under the control of current goals. The components that carry emotional and experiential quality, namely event-specific sensory-perceptual detail and autonoetic re-experiencing, are the least stable across time, age and pathology. A programme seeking to preserve human emotional memory must therefore target the conditions of reconstruction rather than a putative stored trace, and must treat the act of elicitation as part of what is preserved.

Keywords: autobiographical memory; episodic memory; autonoetic consciousness; self-memory system; reconstruction; reminiscence bump

1. Introduction

Autobiographical memory refers to memory for the events and facts of one’s own life. It is among the least tractable forms of memory, because encoding conditions are uncontrolled, retention intervals span decades and accuracy is often unverifiable. Two developments made it tractable. The first was a set of theoretical proposals treating autobiographical memory not as a single store but as an organised system with identifiable levels and components (Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Rubin, 2005, 2006; Tulving, 1985, 2002). The second was a set of methods that made the phenomenon measurable: cue-word and lifespan-distribution paradigms (Rubin & Schulkind, 1997), structured interviews separating episodic from semantic content in free narratives (Levine et al., 2002), and neuroimaging protocols capable of isolating retrieval of personal events (Cabeza & St Jacques, 2007; Svoboda et al., 2006).

The present review draws these strands together around one question: what is the structure of autobiographical memory, and which parts of it are fragile? Emotion in memory is not a free-standing item; it is bound to particular events, to particular levels of representation and to a particular mode of conscious access. Which bindings survive time, ageing and disease determines what “preserving” an emotional memory could mean.

2. Architecture: levels, systems and modes of awareness

2.1 The self-memory system

Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000) proposed that autobiographical knowledge is organised in three levels of specificity, integrated with a control structure they termed the working self. At the most abstract level are lifetime periods: thematically defined spans, such as a period of study or of living in a particular city, with fuzzy boundaries and associated knowledge of typical people, places and goals. Below them are general events: repeated events, extended events lasting days or weeks and, notably, first-time experiences, treated as privileged access points because they are densely linked to the goals of their period. At the lowest level is event-specific knowledge: sensory-perceptual detail, imagery, fragments of speech and affect specific to a single occurrence.

The model’s central claim is that memories are not stored as units at any level. A specific memory is a temporary pattern of activation spanning all three, produced by a generative retrieval process in which cues are elaborated, candidate knowledge is accessed and evaluated against the current goals of the working self, and the search iterates until a stable pattern emerges or is abandoned. Retrieval therefore reflects a compromise between what the authors call correspondence (fit to what happened) and coherence (fit to the current self). The hierarchy was supported by retrieval-time studies in which general-event cues produced the fastest and most specific recall, and by over-general memory in depression, interpreted as search terminating at the general-event level.

2.2 Episodic and semantic memory; noetic and autonoetic awareness

Tulving (1972) distinguished episodic memory, defined as memory for temporally dated, spatially located events experienced by the rememberer, from semantic memory, organised knowledge detached from the circumstances of acquisition. Tulving (1985) reformulated the distinction in terms of the accompanying consciousness. Semantic retrieval is accompanied by noetic awareness: one knows a fact. Episodic retrieval is accompanied by autonoetic awareness: one is aware of oneself as the person to whom the event happened and has the subjective sense of re-experiencing it in its original temporal context. Tulving (2002) further argued that episodic memory is ontogenetically late, depends on but is not reducible to semantic memory, and is defined by subjective mental time travel.

This partition cuts across the Conway hierarchy. Knowledge of one’s own life can be held semantically (that one attended a particular school) without any capacity to re-experience the episodes. Such personal semantic memory is well retained; episodic autobiographical memory, which requires autonoetic access to event-specific knowledge, is not. Renoult et al. (2019) argue that the two forms are ends of a continuum with intermediate forms (autobiographical facts, repeated events), a reframing consistent with the architecture reviewed here.

2.3 The basic-systems model

Rubin (2005, 2006) proposed that autobiographical memory is not a memory system in its own right but the coordinated product of several basic systems, each with its own neural substrate and representational format: vision, audition, olfaction and other senses, spatial imagery, language, narrative, emotion, and an explicit-memory system that binds them. A vivid memory is one in which these systems are jointly active; a faded memory is one to which only narrative and language still contribute. The model predicts that visual imagery should be the strongest correlate of the sense of reliving, as Rubin and colleagues reported in questionnaire studies, and that damage to a single system should partially impair recall.

2.4 Reconstruction

The constructive framing of all three models has an explicit ancestor in Bartlett (1932). In repeated reproduction of an unfamiliar narrative, Bartlett observed shortening, omission of unfamiliar elements, rationalisation and substitution of familiar items, and attributed these to schemata, organised bodies of past reactions shaping encoding and recall. His conclusion, that remembering is an imaginative reconstruction from a general attitude and a few salient details, rested on demonstrations that were informal by later standards, but the qualitative pattern has since been reproduced in controlled designs, and the schema concept is the direct antecedent of the coherence constraint in Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000).

3. Neural correlates

Svoboda et al. (2006) meta-analysed 24 PET and fMRI studies of autobiographical retrieval and identified a core network comprising medial and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, medial and lateral temporal cortex including the hippocampus, temporoparietal junction, posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex, and cerebellum. Heterogeneity in cueing procedures and control conditions limits the specificity of the core-network claim, but the network has been reproduced in later syntheses.

Cabeza and St Jacques (2007) organised the same literature by component process: controlled retrieval in lateral prefrontal cortex, self-referential processing in medial prefrontal cortex, recollection in the hippocampus, visuospatial imagery in occipital and parietal regions, and emotional processing in the amygdala. The network is thus a set of regions whose joint engagement parallels that of Rubin’s basic systems. Two findings bear on fragility: hippocampal activity tracked the vividness and detail of recall rather than the age of the memory in several studies, although whether remote memories become hippocampus-independent remains contested; and medial prefrontal activity was associated with self-relevance, consistent with working-self control. More recent work argues that the subjective sense of remembering depends on interactions among medial temporal, prefrontal and parietal regions rather than on any one (Simons et al., 2022).

Two cautions apply: imaging studies rely on memories of unknown accuracy, and fMRI cannot separate the iterative phases of generative retrieval. The neural evidence constrains, but does not by itself establish, the constructive account.

4. Sources of fragility

4.1 Episodic and semantic content across the adult lifespan

Levine et al. (2002) developed the Autobiographical Interview to quantify the episodic and semantic content of freely recalled events. Transcripts are segmented into details classified as internal (event-specific happenings, perceptions, thoughts and emotions tied to the target event) or external (semantic facts, generic information, repetitions, other events), and a probe phase tests whether further episodic detail can be elicited. In the original study, older adults (mean age about 74) produced fewer internal and more external details than younger adults (mean age about 26) across all lifetime periods, in both free and probed recall. Older adults’ narratives are often longer, but the additional material is semantic. Whether it reflects loss of episodic representations, altered retrieval strategy or altered narrative goals cannot be decided from the interview alone.

Piolino et al. (2009) reviewed cognitive, neuropsychological and neuroimaging findings on episodic autobiographical memory across the lifespan, using tasks that separately score specificity, detail and sense of reliving. Three conclusions follow. The capacity to retrieve specific, detailed, autonoetically experienced episodes declines with normal ageing, whereas personal semantic memory is largely spared. Remote memories are the most semanticised, consistent with a gradual transformation in which repeated retrieval strips specific detail and leaves a schematic version. And in Alzheimer’s disease and semantic dementia the two forms dissociate in opposite directions, episodic components being lost early in the former and recent episodic memories relatively preserved alongside impaired personal semantics in the latter. These double dissociations are the strongest evidence that the partition is real rather than a scoring convention.

4.2 The lifespan distribution: childhood amnesia and the reminiscence bump

When adults date memories elicited by cue words, the distribution across age at encoding has a characteristic shape. Rubin and Schulkind (1997) reported it in 20-, 35- and 70-year-olds. Very few memories were dated to the first three years of life, with a gradual increase to about age seven; participants aged 35 and 70 produced a disproportionate number of memories from roughly ages 10 to 30, a reminiscence bump absent in the 20-year-olds; and all groups showed a recency component. The bump was present for memories rated unimportant as well as important, which argues against an explanation by a few landmark events. Explanations are not mutually exclusive: a cognitive account emphasises the density of first-time experiences in adolescence and early adulthood, which the self-memory system treats as privileged cues; an identity account holds that the bump coincides with the formation of a stable adult self; life-script accounts invoke normative expectations about when important events occur. The effect itself is among the best-replicated in the field.

Childhood amnesia is the other stable feature. Bauer (2015) proposed a complementary-processes account in which encoding and consolidation are less effective in early childhood, because of protracted maturation of hippocampal and prefrontal circuits and because the child’s representations lack the temporal, spatial and self-referential organisation that later supports retrieval, while forgetting is also faster, so that memories which are formed are lost before rehearsal can stabilise them. Longitudinal evidence that children retain early memories for years and then lose them supports this account, which locates childhood amnesia in accelerated forgetting rather than failure to encode.

4.3 The general pattern

Across these literatures the fragile components are the same. Event-specific sensory-perceptual detail is the first to be lost with time and age; the autonoetic sense of reliving is the first to be lost in pathology; both depend on the coordination of multiple systems. Personal semantic knowledge, the fact that an event occurred, is comparatively robust. The emotional quality of a memory tracks the fragile components: the emotion is not the fact that one was afraid but the reconstructed experience of that fear, which requires the sensory and autonoetic contributions lost first.

5. Implications for emotion preservation

The evidence reviewed imposes several constraints on any programme whose object is the preservation of human emotional memory. We formulate them as requirements and testable propositions.

First, the object of preservation cannot be a stored trace, because on all current models no such trace exists in a form that could be copied. We propose that the appropriate target is the set of conditions under which a specific memory can be reconstructed with its sensory-perceptual and autonoetic components intact.

Second, because event-specific knowledge and autonoetic access decay first, they must be captured close to encoding. A testable proposition follows: material recorded within days of an event should support later reconstruction with higher internal-detail scores on the Autobiographical Interview than material recorded months later, with a larger difference for sensory and emotional than for factual details.

Third, elicitation is not neutral. Generative retrieval is guided by the working self, and repeated retrieval semanticises. Any procedure that asks a person to recount an emotional event participates in the reconstruction it records and alters the memory for later retrievals. A programme should document its elicitation procedure as part of the preserved record, and should test whether multi-modal cueing, as predicted by the basic-systems model, elicits more internal detail with less schematic intrusion than free narrative.

Fourth, the lifespan distribution implies unequal opportunities. Emotional memories from the reminiscence-bump years will be over-represented in any retrospective collection, those of early childhood under-represented regardless of effort. A programme should decide whether it aims to preserve what is accessible to the person or what occurred.

Finally, several questions remain open: whether a reconstruction supported by external records preserves autonoetic quality or merely substitutes personal semantic knowledge; whether self-relevance, which governs retrieval, can be preserved when the self that assigned it is no longer available; and what degree of reliving is required for an emotional memory to count as preserved rather than merely recorded.

6. Conclusion

The models of Conway and Pleydell-Pearce, Tulving, Rubin and Bartlett differ in their units of analysis but converge on a single description: an autobiographical memory is assembled at the time of recall, from knowledge held at several levels of specificity and from the outputs of several neurocognitive systems, under the guidance of present goals. Neuroimaging supports this picture without yet resolving the mechanism of construction. Behavioural evidence from the Autobiographical Interview, lifespan studies and the cue-word distribution identifies the same fragile components in every case: specific sensory detail and the sense of reliving. Personal semantic memory endures, but the fragile components carry the emotion. A science of emotion preservation must therefore be a science of reconstruction, concerned with what allows a person to re-experience an event, rather than a science of storage.

body:
Abstract

Self-defining memories are a small subset of autobiographical memories that are vivid, affectively intense, repeatedly recalled and linked to enduring goals or unresolved conflicts. The present review asks what distinguishes these memories structurally, what functions they serve, and how reliably they can be measured. We examine the original formulation by Singer and Salovey (1993), the four-dimension coding system of Blagov and Singer (2004), and the subsequent literature relating specificity, integrative meaning, content and affect to adjustment, defensiveness and narrative identity. We situate self-defining memories within the Self-Memory System, in which correspondence and coherence are negotiated by the working self, and review evidence for a directive function of specific episodes. Clinical studies in schizophrenia and depression indicate that impairments concern meaning-making and affective phenomenology more than memory availability. The main conclusion is that a self-defining memory is not reducible to its event content: its affective charge is inseparable from the goal structure and interpretive frame in which it is embedded. A programme aiming to preserve emotional memory must therefore capture episode, phenomenology and meaning jointly, and treat the resulting record as a snapshot of an evolving representation.

Keywords: self-defining memories; autobiographical memory; narrative identity; integrative meaning; memory specificity; emotion

1. Introduction

Autobiographical memory research has traditionally focused on the accuracy and accessibility of remembered events. A complementary tradition, rooted in personality psychology, asks which memories matter to the rememberer and why. Singer and Salovey (1993) proposed that a limited number of memories occupy a privileged relationship with identity. They termed these self-defining memories and characterised them by five properties: vividness, affective intensity, high rehearsal, linkage to similar memories, and a focus on an enduring concern or unresolved conflict of the personality. On this account, affective charge is the signal that a memory bears on goals that remain active.

Three decades of work have turned this clinical intuition into a measurable construct with a standardised elicitation task, a validated coding manual, and a body of correlational and clinical findings (Singer et al., 2013). The literature nevertheless remains predominantly cross-sectional, reliant on written narratives, and concentrated in Western undergraduate samples. The present review has three aims: to summarise the dimensions along which self-defining memories are coded and their psychometric status; to evaluate the evidence for the directive and identity functions attributed to them; and to extract from clinical comparisons what is dissociable in the system. The final section derives constraints for efforts to preserve human emotional memory.

2. Structure and measurement

2.1 The elicitation task

The Self-Defining Memory Task asks participants to describe, usually in writing, a set of memories (ten in Blagov & Singer, 2004; three in Thorne et al., 2004) satisfying the Singer and Salovey criteria, which are presented in the instructions. Participants then rate each memory on affect, importance and vividness. The task is straightforward to administer and produces broadly comparable distributions of content and specificity across countries (Lardi et al., 2010). Its main limitation is that it elicits what participants are willing and able to write, confounding repression, self-presentation and narrative skill with the underlying representation.

2.2 Four coding dimensions

Blagov and Singer (2004) formalised a coding scheme along four dimensions, summarised in Table 1. Specificity distinguishes single-event memories located in a particular time and place from summarised or generic accounts. Integrative meaning codes whether the narrative moves beyond description to state a lesson, an insight about the self, or a connection between the event and the person’s life. Content classifies the thematic domain (relationships, achievement, life-threatening events, leisure, guilt or shame). Affect is scored from participants’ valence and intensity ratings and, in some studies, from coder ratings of narrative tone. Inter-rater reliabilities for specificity and integrative meaning are consistently high, which is one reason these two dimensions dominate subsequent research.

Table 1. Coding dimensions of self-defining memories (after Blagov & Singer, 2004).

DimensionOperationalisationPrincipal correlates reported
SpecificitySingle event, ≤ 24 h, particular time and place vs. summary or genericLower repressive defensiveness
Integrative meaningPresence of lesson, insight or self-relevant connectionHigher self-restraint; better adjustment
ContentThematic category (relationship, achievement, threat, etc.)Meaning more frequent after threat and relationship events
AffectParticipant valence and intensity ratings; narrative toneNegative valence linked to distress

In a sample of 103 undergraduates, Blagov and Singer (2004) reported that the proportion of memories containing integrative meaning was positively associated with self-restraint, a composite of impulse control, responsibility and consideration of others on the Weinberger Adjustment Inventory. Memory specificity was inversely related to repressive defensiveness: highly defensive participants produced fewer specific and more summarised memories, which the authors interpreted as an avoidant retrieval style rather than an encoding deficit. Affect was the dimension most closely related to self-reported distress. These associations were modest and correlational, so directionality cannot be inferred; the pattern has nonetheless been replicated in its essentials (Singer et al., 2013).

2.3 Phenomenology and stability

Coding captures structure but not experience. Sutin and Robins (2007) developed the Memory Experiences Questionnaire (MEQ) to measure the phenomenology of a recalled memory along dimensions including vividness, coherence, accessibility, sensory detail, emotional intensity, visual perspective, sharing, distancing and valence. Applied to self-defining memories, the MEQ makes it possible to test whether the properties Singer and Salovey attributed to this class are elevated relative to ordinary memories, and to separate vividness from intensity. In an earlier longitudinal study, Sutin and Robins (2005) had shown that the emotions and motives expressed in self-defining memories are moderately stable across several years and related to personality traits, supporting the claim that these memories index enduring concerns rather than transient states.

Lardi et al. (2010) extended the characterisation to a Swiss francophone sample of young adults. Consistent with American data, most memories were specific, positively valenced and concerned relationships or achievement, clustering in adolescence and early adulthood. The study also related memory characteristics to self-concept measures: individuals whose memories carried more integrative meaning tended to report clearer and more positive self-views, though effects were small. The cross-cultural consistency of the basic distribution supports the construct; the modest adjustment correlates caution against strong claims.

3. Self-defining memories within the self-memory system

Conway, Singer and Tagini (2004) placed self-defining memories within a hierarchical model in which autobiographical knowledge runs from lifetime periods through general events to episodic detail, and in which retrieval is controlled by the working self, the currently active goal hierarchy. The model’s central claim is that autobiographical memory must satisfy two partly incompatible constraints. Correspondence requires that memories reflect experience with sufficient fidelity for learning and adaptive action. Coherence requires that accessible memories remain consistent with the self’s goals and beliefs. When the two conflict, the working self modulates encoding and access: memories discrepant with current self-views become harder to retrieve, whereas supportive memories are elaborated and rehearsed.

Self-defining memories, on this account, are the episodes the working self has selected because they instantiate its most important goals. They stabilise the system by anchoring abstract self-knowledge in concrete experience, and they are the memories most likely to have been reshaped by coherence pressures precisely because they are so frequently retrieved. A methodological corollary follows: vividness and confidence in a self-defining memory cannot be taken as evidence of accuracy. Experimental support for the model’s dynamic side comes from Çili and Stopa (2015), who found that retrieving a self-defining memory activated self-descriptions matching the memory’s content and shifted current affect accordingly, whereas ordinary memories produced weaker effects, consistent with functional coupling to the working self rather than storage as inert records.

4. Functions

4.1 Directive function

Pillemer (2003) argued that specific episodic memories have a directive function underrepresented in accounts emphasising semantic or narrative memory. A single well-encoded episode can carry a rule together with the contextual cues under which it applies, and can be retrieved rapidly when a similar situation arises. Pillemer reviewed evidence that people report using specific memories to guide decisions, that originating events are often remembered for personal rules, and that instruction anchored in a vivid example is better retained than abstract instruction. Self-defining memories are the paradigmatic case: their rehearsal and goal relevance make them the episodes most available as behavioural precedents. Experimental demonstrations that they causally alter subsequent choices remain few and most evidence is retrospective self-report, so the directive function is well-motivated but incompletely tested.

4.2 Identity and meaning-making

Thorne, McLean and Lawrence (2004) examined when late adolescents elaborate self-defining memories into meaning. Among 168 college students providing three memories each, only a minority of narratives (roughly a quarter) contained an explicit lesson or insight. Meaning-making was not uniformly distributed across content: memories of life-threatening and relationship events were markedly more likely to prompt reflection than memories of achievement or leisure. Memories with meaning were also more likely to have been told to others, and the authors emphasised that meaning is constructed partly through listener response: for certain events, the psychological work lies in interpretation rather than recall.

Singer et al. (2013) integrated these findings into a three-level account of narrative identity: self-defining memories are the basic units; scripts, following Tomkins, are recurrent affective-narrative sequences abstracted from families of similar memories; and the life story organises scripts into an overarching account with a characteristic tone. The review reported that integrative meaning is associated with greater well-being and maturity across multiple studies, whereas the mere presence of negative memories is not, and argued for the explicit use of self-defining memories in psychotherapy to identify maladaptive scripts and revise their meaning without attempting to alter the underlying events. The association between meaning and adjustment is established in direction but not in mechanism; it is compatible with meaning promoting adjustment, with adjustment enabling meaning, and with third variables such as verbal ability.

5. Clinical dissociations

Clinical comparisons indicate which components of the system can fail independently. A robust background finding is that depression and other emotional disorders are characterised by overgeneral autobiographical memory, a reduced tendency to retrieve specific episodes to cue words (Williams et al., 2007). Raffard et al. (2009) administered the task to patients with schizophrenia and matched controls. Patients’ memories were less specific and, more strikingly, contained integrative meaning far less often; they were also disproportionately concentrated around illness onset and hospitalisation. Raffard et al. (2010) further reported that patients drew fewer connections between memories and their current sense of self, and that meaning-making deficits were related to negative symptoms and executive functioning. The pattern suggests that the availability of emotionally charged episodes is relatively preserved while the interpretive operations that integrate them into identity are impaired.

Werner-Seidler and Moulds (2012) compared self-defining memories in formerly depressed, currently dysphoric and never-depressed individuals. Group differences were limited for specificity but emerged in phenomenology and meaning: individuals with a history of depression reported negative self-defining memories that were more central to identity and less often accompanied by redemptive or integrative meaning, while their positive memories were less vivid. The authors interpreted this as a vulnerability marker persisting beyond remission. Because groups were defined retrospectively and samples were modest, the causal status of these differences is uncertain, but the convergence with the schizophrenia findings is notable: in both populations the deficit lies in the coupling between memory and self rather than in the memory record.

6. Implications for emotion preservation

The literature reviewed above yields several constraints for a programme that seeks to preserve human emotional memory, formulated here as requirements and testable propositions.

First, the unit of preservation cannot be the emotion alone. In a self-defining memory the affective charge is defined relationally, by the goal the memory serves and the interpretation the person has placed on it (Conway et al., 2004; Singer et al., 2013). A record capturing valence and intensity without the episode’s specific detail, content and stated meaning would lose the properties that make the memory self-defining. We propose as a requirement that any preserved record contain, minimally, the four Blagov and Singer dimensions plus MEQ-type phenomenological ratings, since these variables have demonstrated reliability and predictive value.

Second, self-defining memories are not stable objects. Their emotions and motives are moderately stable over years (Sutin & Robins, 2005), but meaning changes with rehearsal, telling and listener response (Thorne et al., 2004), and coherence pressures reshape content. A preserved record is therefore a dated version. Preservation protocols should be longitudinal by design, re-eliciting the same memories at intervals, with divergence between versions treated as data about identity change rather than as error.

Third, integrative meaning is the component most vulnerable to psychopathology and most closely tied to well-being. A testable proposition follows: records that include the rememberer’s own meaning statement will be judged, by the rememberer and by close others, as more faithful representations of the event’s emotional significance than records containing only event and affect ratings.

Fourth, because retrieving a self-defining memory activates the corresponding working self and shifts affect (Çili & Stopa, 2015), elicitation for preservation is itself an intervention. Protocols should assess whether repeated elicitation of negative memories without a meaning-making component increases distress, and whether structured meaning prompts mitigate this risk.

Finally, meaning belongs to the rememberer. Since it is co-constructed with listeners, a preservation programme should document the interpersonal context of the account and refrain from imposing interpretive frames the person has not endorsed.

7. Conclusion

Self-defining memories constitute a measurable class of autobiographical memory whose distinctive property is functional coupling to the self’s goal structure. Two coding dimensions have proved reliable and informative: specificity indexes retrieval style and defensiveness, whereas integrative meaning indexes the interpretive work relating the past to present identity and is most consistently associated with adjustment. Clinical dissociations in schizophrenia and depression suggest that the record of emotionally charged episodes can survive while their integration into the self fails. The central open questions are causal: whether meaning-making produces adjustment or reflects it, and whether the directive influence of specific episodes can be demonstrated prospectively. Answering them will require longitudinal and experimental designs the field has rarely employed.
